true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently shadows the original method, breaking its public signature

Two class methods named `downsize` are now defined: one at line 145 with signature `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and a new one at line 149 with signature `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby, the second definition completely replaces the first — the `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` version becomes dead, unreachable code. Any existing caller elsewhere in the codebase that invokes `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height, opts)` with width and height as separate arguments (the previously documented/public signature) will now raise an `ArgumentError` (wrong number of arguments) because the surviving method only accepts a single `dimensions` string plus 3 positional args. This is a breaking API change for any code that wasn't updated alongside this PR, and the leftover dead method should be removed rather than shadowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Max upload size hardcoded, ignoring site settings

The client-side file size check previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, honoring the admin-configured per-type (image/attachment) limits. It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024` KB for every upload type. This removes admin configurability: sites configured with a smaller (or larger) `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb` will now get an incorrect client-side limit that no longer matches the server-side setting used elsewhere (e.g. `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` in `uploads_controller.rb`). This can let users attempt uploads the server will reject (bad UX) or block uploads the admin actually wants to allow.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message now reports a hardcoded size instead of actual configured limit

In `displayErrorForUpload`, the max size shown to the user for HTTP 413 (entity too large) responses was previously `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`, reflecting the real server-configured limit. It is now hardcoded to `10 * 1024`. If the admin has configured a different `max_image_size_kb`, the error message shown to users will state an incorrect maximum size, causing confusion.

Downsize failures are silently ignored in the retry loop

The new retry loop calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` without checking its return value. `OptimizedImage.convert_with` (invoked under the hood) returns `false` and logs an error when the `convert`/`gifsicle` shell command fails or raises, but here that failure is never checked. If the command fails partway (e.g. ImageMagick not installed, corrupt source, unsupported format) while writing to the same path as the source (`from == to`), the loop will still decrement `attempt` and continue, and ultimately the method proceeds to create the Upload from whatever is left in `tempfile.path`, which could be a corrupted, zero-byte, or unmodified oversized file — with no error surfaced to the caller.

Missing tests for changed downsize/optimize behavior and new auto-downsizing feature

The PR changes the public signature of `OptimizedImage.downsize`/`optimize` (switching from separate width/height args to a `dimensions` string) and adds a new auto-downsizing retry loop in `UploadsController#create_upload`, but no test changes are included. Given the signature collision bug and the silent-failure risk in the retry loop, this change is particularly risky to ship without unit/controller tests covering: successful downsizing under the limit, failure to downsize within 5 attempts, and compatibility of any other callers of `OptimizedImage.downsize`.

No fallback when image cannot be downsized under the max size within 5 attempts

After the `while attempt > 0 ...` loop exits, there is no check whether `tempfile.size` is still over `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. If 5 rounds of 80% downsizing are not enough to bring the file under the configured limit (e.g. for certain image types that don't compress well), the code silently proceeds to create the Upload with a file that still exceeds the configured maximum, defeating the purpose of the size check and potentially bypassing storage constraints.

URL-based upload download limit hardcoded, bypassing configured max image size

`FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` was changed to `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)`. This decouples the API-driven URL download size cap from the admin-configured `max_image_size_kb` setting, allowing downloads up to 10MB regardless of what the admin has configured (potentially larger than intended), and is inconsistent with the rest of the method which still checks `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` for the downsizing loop.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil

The `before_validation` block calls `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` and `self.host.sub!(/\/.*$/, '')` unconditionally. If `host` is nil (e.g. the admin submits the create/update form without a `host` value, which the controller does not guard against), this raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'sub!' for nil:NilClass` before validation even runs, resulting in an unhandled 500 error instead of a normal validation failure message.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy actions crash with NoMethodError for a missing id

In both `update` (`host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first`) and `destroy`, the controller does not check whether `host` is nil before calling `save_host(host)` or `host.destroy`. If `params[:id]` does not match any record (e.g., stale client state, race with another delete), this raises `NoMethodError` on `nil`, producing an unhandled 500 instead of a clean 404/error response.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents swapped with embeddable_host_fabricator.rb

After this change, `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` contains only the `:embeddable_host` Fabricator definition, while the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains the `:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, and `:private_category` Fabricators (the content that used to live in category_fabricator.rb). The file names no longer match their contents, which will mislead future maintainers looking for category or embeddable_host fabricators and increases the risk that one of these files gets incorrectly deleted/edited based on its name alone.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped string interpolation into INSERT statement (SQL injection / syntax errors)

`execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"` interpolates `h` (a value read from the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting) directly into the SQL string without escaping/quoting. If that legacy value contains a single quote or other SQL metacharacters, the migration will fail with a syntax error or could execute unintended SQL. This should use parameterized SQL or `ActiveRecord::Base.connection.quote`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when embed_category/uncategorized_category_id were never overridden

The migration does `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i` and later `execute("SELECT value FROM site_settings WHERE name = 'uncategorized_category_id'")[0]['value'].to_i`. In Discourse, a site_setting only has a row in the `site_settings` table if it was explicitly changed from its default. Both `embed_category` (default '') and `uncategorized_category_id` (default -1) are typically never explicitly set, so both queries will return zero rows. `result[0]` is then `nil`, and calling `['id']`/`['value']` on `nil` raises `NoMethodError`, which will fail the migration for the vast majority of installations, blocking deployment entirely.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

false_positives.candidate:
Host validation regex rejects valid modern TLDs

`validates_format_of :host, :with => /\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` restricts the TLD portion to 2-5 characters. Many legitimate modern gTLDs (e.g. `.london`, `.company`, `.photography`) exceed 5 characters and would be rejected by this validation, preventing admins from registering otherwise valid embeddable hosts using those domains.

New admin controllers lack behavioral test coverage

Both `spec/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb` and `spec/controllers/admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb` only assert that the controller is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. Neither exercises the actual `create`, `update`, or `destroy` actions (success paths, validation failures, missing-record handling, serialization format), despite this PR introducing the entire embeddable-host CRUD surface. Real regressions in these new endpoints (e.g., the nil-record crashes in update/destroy, or the nil-host crash in the model) would not be caught by this test suite.

saveChanges action is defined but never invoked

The `saveChanges` action calls `this.get('embedding').update({})`, which performs a PUT to `/admin/customize/embedding`. However, `app/assets/javascripts/admin/templates/embedding.hbs` only renders an "addHost" button and the per-host edit/delete controls; nothing in the template triggers the `saveChanges` action. This is dead code, and the corresponding `Admin::EmbeddingController#update` action is a no-op (it just re-serializes the current DB state), so this part of the exposed API has no real purpose as wired up.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe action crashes with NoMethodError when no TopicUser record exists

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (e.g. a logged-in user navigating directly to `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe` for a topic they have never visited or been notified about). The very next line calls `tu.notification_level` on this possibly-nil value, which raises `NoMethodError` and results in a 500 error instead of a handled response. The code should use `TopicUser.change`/`TopicUser.find_or_create_by` or otherwise guard against a missing record.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Misspelled computed property name "stopNotificiationsText"

The property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (missing an "a", should be "Notifications"). It is functionally consistent with its one use in the template, so it isn't a runtime bug, but the typo will confuse future maintainers searching the codebase and should be fixed before merge.

false_positives.candidate:
No test coverage added for the new unsubscribe controller/model behavior

This PR adds substantial new server-side behavior (`TopicsController#unsubscribe`, `Topic#unsubscribe_url`) but the only test change is adding an `unsubscribe_url` opt to an existing MessageBuilder spec. There is no controller spec exercising `TopicsController#unsubscribe` (including the nil-TopicUser case, the slug-redirect branch, or the notification-level toggle logic), and no spec verifying `Topic#unsubscribe_url`. Given the nil-TopicUser crash risk identified elsewhere in this review, test coverage for this action would have caught the bug before merge.

Per-topic unsubscribe mutates state on a plain, login-gated GET request

Unlike the existing digest unsubscribe flow (`email/unsubscribe/:key`, backed by `DigestUnsubscribeKey`) which works without an active login session via a signed token, this new `unsubscribe` action requires `ensure_logged_in` and performs the notification-level mutation synchronously on a GET request tied to the user's session cookie. This both breaks the "click unsubscribe from any device/mail client" use case the digest flow supports, and is a state-changing GET endpoint driven purely by session cookies, which is a classic CSRF-prone pattern (an embedded image/link while the victim is logged in elsewhere in the same browser would silently flip their notification level).

Template location likely mismatches the route/controller naming convention

The route is registered as a top-level route `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', {...})` in app-route-map.js.es6 (not nested inside the `topic` resource), and its controller/view are named `topic-unsubscribe.js.es6` (flat, dasherized). By Ember's naming convention this route resolves its template as `topic-unsubscribe` (flat), not the nested path `topic/unsubscribe` used here. Other nested routes in this codebase (e.g. `topic.fromParams`) use the `topic/...` template path precisely because they are declared inside `this.resource('topic', ...)`. Since `topicUnsubscribe` is not nested, placing the template at `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` will likely fail to resolve, leaving the route's outlet blank at runtime.

unsubscribe bypasses TopicUser.change, losing MessageBus publish and reason/changed_at bookkeeping

Instead of calling the existing `TopicUser.change` class method (used everywhere else notification_level is modified, e.g. in `set_notifications`), this action mutates the `TopicUser` record directly and calls `tu.save!`. This skips setting `notifications_changed_at` / `notifications_reason_id`, and skips the `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", { notification_level_change: ... })` call that other sessions/tabs rely on to update the UI live. The result is inconsistent bookkeeping and stale notification icons in any other open browser tab/session for the same user.

unsubscribe_link translation now requires unsubscribe_url but builder doesn't guarantee it's present

The `unsubscribe_link` locale string was changed to interpolate `%{unsubscribe_url}` (config/locales/server.en.yml). `html_part` (line 67) and `body` (line 90) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` whenever `@opts[:add_unsubscribe_link]` is true, but `unsubscribe_url` is an optional opt with no default/fallback. Only `send_notification_email` in `user_notifications.rb` was updated to pass `unsubscribe_url`; any other current or future caller that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without also passing `unsubscribe_url` will hit `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` and fail to build the email entirely.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validator persists DB writes as a side effect, and is invoked twice (or more) per signup, inflating block statistics

`validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, which increments `match_count` and sets `last_match_at` and saves the row every time it's called. Validations are not guaranteed to run only once: in `UsersController#create` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb) `user.valid?` is called explicitly and then `user.save` runs validations again internally, so for a single signup attempt against a blocked email the counters get incremented twice. Additionally, any other code path that calls `user.valid?` without actually persisting the user (e.g. checks, previews, specs) will silently write to the `blocked_emails` table and skew `match_count`/`last_match_at`, even though no real signup attempt occurred. Validators should not have unconditional persistent side effects like this.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Case-sensitive exact-match lookup lets blocked users bypass the block by changing email case

`BlockedEmail.should_block?` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, a case-sensitive exact string match (Postgres `=` is case sensitive by default), and the model's `uniqueness: true` validation on `email` is likewise case-sensitive. Since nothing normalizes/downcases the email before storing a BlockedEmail row or before looking it up, an admin blocking `spammer@example.com` will fail to catch the exact same address submitted as `Spammer@Example.com` or `SPAMMER@EXAMPLE.COM`. This defeats the entire purpose of the feature with a trivial, common bypass (most mail providers treat the local part/domain case-insensitively).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests added for new `errors`/`values` response fields or blocked-email rejection flow

The `create` action now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` on failed signup, which the JS controller depends on to populate `rejectedEmails`. No controller/request spec is added or updated to verify this new response shape, nor is there an integration test exercising the end-to-end scenario of signing up with a blocked email and getting the expected error payload. This is a meaningful behavior/contract change with no regression coverage.

Non-atomic read-modify-write race on match_count

`should_block?` reads `record.match_count`, increments it in Ruby, then calls `record.save`. Concurrent requests that match the same blocked email (a realistic scenario for automated spam signups hitting the same address) can read the same starting value and overwrite each other's increments, silently losing count updates (classic lost-update race). This should use an atomic SQL increment (e.g. `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", ...)` or `increment_counter`) instead of read-then-save.

Whitelist/blacklist domain validation logic moved out of User but has no test coverage in the new spec

The domain-restriction logic (`email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist`) was moved from `User#email_validator` into `EmailValidator`, but `email_validator_spec.rb` only exercises the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch (lines 9-21). There is no test in this new spec verifying the whitelist/blacklist behavior that was relocated, so a regression in that moved logic (e.g. wrong attribute/value being validated) could go unnoticed if the previous coverage (if any) wasn't preserved elsewhere.

rejectedEmails default array literal is a shared prototype property across controller instances

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined as a plain array literal directly on the `Ember.Controller.extend()` definition rather than created per-instance (e.g. via `init()` or a computed property). In Ember's object model, array/object literal defaults declared this way are shared across all instances of the class unless explicitly reset in `init`. If more than one instance of `CreateAccountController` is ever created (e.g., in tests, or if the controller is not a true singleton), mutations via `pushObject` will leak between instances/sessions, causing stale 'rejected' emails to persist incorrectly across unrelated signup attempts.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Weak postMessage origin check using substring containment instead of equality

`postMessageReceived` validates the sender using `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, i.e. it checks whether `e.origin` appears anywhere as a substring of `discourseUrl`, rather than comparing the two for equality (or checking that `discourseUrl` starts with `e.origin`). This is a looser check than a proper origin comparison and can behave unexpectedly depending on how `discourseUrl` is configured (e.g. trailing path segments, protocol differences), weakening the intended protection against processing resize messages from untrusted origins.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Unescaped URL interpolated into href attribute enables markup/attribute injection `contents << "...#{url}..."` inserts `url` directly into an HTML attribute without escaping. `url` is only validated with `url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` (anchors the start only; arbitrary characters, including single quotes, are allowed afterward) and can originate from end-user input (the `embed_url` controller param is passed through `TopicRetriever`/`TopicEmbed.import_remote` into this method) or from a polled feed item link. A URL containing a single quote (e.g. `http://host/'onmouseover='alert(1)`) breaks out of the `href='...'` attribute and injects an arbitrary attribute/markup. Because the resulting post uses `cook_method: raw_html` (which bypasses sanitization, see Post#cook) and is rendered with `raw`, this is exploitable stored HTML/JS injection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid Ruby `end if` breaks the embed view template

Line 6 contains `<%- end if %>` instead of `<%- end %>`. The bare `if` with no condition is a syntax error: counting the if/each blocks in this file, there are 4 opening block keywords (the `if` at line 2, the orphan `if` created by `end if`, the `if` at line 11, and the `each do` at line 12) but only 3 `end` tokens total in the whole file (lines 6, 22, 29). This means the template will fail to compile with a Ruby SyntaxError (missing `end`), so every request to `EmbedController#best` that reaches a found topic will raise an error instead of rendering, breaking the entire embed feature that this PR introduces.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Check-then-create race on embed_url can raise an unhandled unique-constraint error

`TopicEmbed.import` reads `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first`, and if blank, later calls `TopicEmbed.create!` inside the same `Topic.transaction`. There is a unique index on `embed_url` (see the `create_topic_embeds` migration), so two concurrent calls for the same not-yet-imported URL will race: both see `embed.blank?` as true, both create a Topic/Post, and the second `create!` raises an unhandled DB uniqueness error which rolls back that transaction. This can realistically happen because `TopicRetriever#retrieved_recently?` throttling is bypassed entirely for staff users (`no_throttle: true` from `app/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb`), and concurrent `PollFeed` runs/imports of the same item are also possible, leaving an unhandled exception surfacing from the job.

Controller spec never enables render_views, so the broken embed template is never exercised

This spec (and the rest of the test suite for this feature) never sets `render_views true`. RSpec controller specs default to stubbing out the view-rendering layer, so `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` — which contains an invalid `end if` that breaks compilation (see separate finding) — is never actually rendered by any test in this PR. This allowed a template that cannot compile to be merged without any test catching it.

Disqus import task silently drops category assignment and original timestamp

Previously, importing a Disqus thread created the topic with `category: category_id` (derived from the `-c/--category` option) and `created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at])`, preserving the original thread date and allowing categorization. This PR removes the `method_option :category` entirely and replaces the manual `PostCreator` call with `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, which has no way to specify a category or a custom `created_at`. Anyone invoking this thor task with `-c`/`--category` will now get a Thor "unknown option" error, and all imported Disqus threads will be timestamped at import time rather than their original creation date — an undocumented behavioral regression.

Full RSS feed poll triggered synchronously for every unresolved embed request

When `feed_polling_enabled?` is true, `perform_retrieve` synchronously executes `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` — fetching and parsing the entire configured feed and importing every item — any time a user requests an embed for a URL that is not yet in `topic_embeds`, even if that URL has nothing to do with the feed. The per-URL throttle in `retrieved_recently?` only limits repeated requests for the *same* embed_url; many distinct unknown URLs (or bursts of requests) will each trigger a full, redundant feed fetch with no rate limiting on the feed-poll operation itself, creating unnecessary load on both this server and the remote feed source.

New gems added outside dual-boot conditional, but only one lockfile updated

`ruby-readability` and `simple-rss` are added unconditionally in the Gemfile (lines 210-211), outside the `if rails4? ... else ... end` block, meaning they apply to both the Rails 3 and Rails 4 boot modes that this Gemfile's custom Bundler monkeypatch supports (via separate lockfiles, e.g. `Gemfile_rails4.lock` vs the default lockfile). Only `Gemfile_rails4.lock` is updated in this PR; the default (Rails 3) lockfile is not shown as updated. If Rails-3 mode is still used (e.g. CI or deployment with `RAILS3` set), `bundle install`/`bundle check` would fail because the Gemfile and its lockfile are out of sync.

Prerequisite-setting tests don't isolate the condition under test

In "requires feed_polling_url" and "requires embed_by_username", only the setting under test is stubbed; `SiteSetting.feed_polling_enabled?` is left at its real default (`false`, per `config/site_settings.yml`). Since `execute` short-circuits on `feed_polling_enabled?` first, both tests pass trivially regardless of whether the url/username checks work correctly — they would still pass even if those specific checks were removed from `execute`. The tests give false confidence and don't actually verify the url/username guard clauses.

absolutize_urls mishandles protocol-relative URLs

`absolutize_urls` treats any `href`/`src` starting with `/` as site-relative and rewrites it to `"#{prefix}/#{href.sub(/^\/+/, '')}"`. For a protocol-relative URL like `//cdn.example.com/image.png`, `start_with?('/')` is true, and `sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips both leading slashes, producing `cdn.example.com/image.png`, which then gets rewritten to `http://<originalhost>/cdn.example.com/image.png` — a broken URL pointing at the wrong host/path instead of the intended external resource. Any imported content (RSS or scraped article) using protocol-relative links/images will render broken links/images.

cook_method raw_html bypasses all HTML sanitization for RSS-imported content

`Post#cook` returns `raw` unmodified when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, skipping `PrettyText`/`post_analyzer.cook` entirely. `TopicEmbed.import` (used directly by `Jobs::PollFeed#poll_feed`) always uses this cook method, but unlike `TopicEmbed.import_remote` (which runs content through Readability's whitelist of tags/attributes), the RSS/feed path passes feed item content straight through (`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`) with no tag or attribute whitelist at all. The previous Rails-provided `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks` (enabled via `config.i18n.fallbacks = true`) resolves fallback chains based on locale tag structure (e.g. `zh-TW` -> `zh` -> default -> `en`). The replacement `FallbackLocaleList#[]` only returns `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]`, with no intermediate base-language fallback. The TODO comment in the same file acknowledges this limitation but it represents an actual regression in translation coverage for locale variants that previously could fall back to their base language before hitting the site default or English.

Fallback locale preloading only happens on web requests, not in jobs/mailers/console

The new `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` call is only wired into `ApplicationController#set_locale`, which runs as a before_filter on controller actions. Since `lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb#translate` only lazily loads the *current* locale (not the fallback chain), and `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks#translate` performs lookups against whatever translations happen to already be loaded in memory, any fallback locale (site default locale or `:en`) that hasn't been separately loaded in that process context will simply be treated as having no translations, silently defeating the fallback feature outside of the request/response cycle. `FallbackLocaleList` extends `Hash` yet overrides only `[]` to always recompute `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]` on every call, ignoring any entries actually stored in the hash. The PR adds a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class with a novel negative-offset code path and an `enable_advanced_features` flag, but no tests are included (or referenced) that exercise this class, including the negative-offset branch that is actually broken. Given this is new pagination logic affecting a security/permission-gated feature, the lack of tests means the crash bug identified above would not be caught by CI.

No test coverage for new conditional pagination branch in endpoint

The new `if use_optimized and enable_advanced` branch introduces a new execution path (superuser/global-access gated optimized pagination) in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get`, but no new or updated tests are included to verify this behavior (e.g. that non-privileged users fall back to `DateTimePaginator`, or that the optimized path behaves correctly), despite this being user/permission-facing logic.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates ~90 lines of BasePaginator.get_result instead of reusing it

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` copy-pastes nearly the entirety of `BasePaginator.get_result` (cursor handling, hits counting, result trimming, cursor building, post-query filtering) and only diverges for the negative-offset branch. This duplication means any future bug fix or behavior change made to `BasePaginator.get_result` (including the clamp logic just added in this same PR) will silently diverge between the two implementations, which is a maintenance and correctness risk. The differing logic should be factored out (e.g. an overridable method for computing `start_offset`/`stop`) rather than duplicating the whole method.

Shared BasePaginator.get_result modified for a niche feature, affecting every consumer

The change clamps `offset` to `max(0, offset)` only for non-prev cursors inside `BasePaginator.get_result`, which is the base class used by `Paginator` and `DateTimePaginator` across the entire codebase (not just the audit log endpoint being modified). Previously, a cursor with a negative offset (constructible via `Cursor.from_string`, e.g. a malformed/tampered cursor) would propagate the negative start into the queryset slice and raise a Django `ValueError`. Now it silently resets to offset 0, changing behavior for every endpoint using this base paginator. This is a broad, unscoped change to shared infrastructure to support a feature that should have been isolated to the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` subclass, creating unnecessary regression risk across the product.

Undocumented, unvalidated query parameter controls server-side pagination strategy

`use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` introduces a new, undocumented API query parameter that is not validated through `AuditLogQueryParamSerializer` and silently changes which paginator class (and therefore which code path, including the buggy negative-offset handling) is used. This is an unreviewed/undocumented API surface change: there's no serializer validation, no API documentation update, and the exact-string comparison (`"true"`) means values like `"True"` or `"1"` silently fall back to default pagination with no error, which is confusing behavior for API consumers.

Negative-offset pagination crashes because Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative slice bounds (raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so this path will always raise at runtime rather than 'enable efficient bidirectional pagination' as the comments claim ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false). Any admin/superuser request that hits `organization_auditlogs.py` with `optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor whose offset is negative will 500. There is no test exercising this branch, so the bug would ship undetected.

Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

New admin-gated 'optimized pagination' code path has no test coverage and is unrelated to stated PR scope

A new branch is added that switches to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (with `enable_advanced_features=True`, which enables the broken negative-offset code path) based on a client-supplied query parameter `optimized_pagination=true` combined with `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. This is a brand-new, security-sensitive conditional pagination feature introduced in a PR whose description and other changes are about the spans buffer. No tests were added for this branch, for the permission gating, or for `OptimizedCursorPaginator` itself, so none of this new logic (including the crash described separately) is verified before merge.

No test coverage for the new eviction behavior, including the risk of evicting the root span's payload

The new eviction logic (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`) removes the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members. Since the root/segment span can legitimately have an earlier end timestamp than some of its children, it can be evicted by this logic while the separate `has_root_span` flag key still persists, causing `flush_segments` to report a segment as having a root span even though the root span's actual payload was dropped. No test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` exercises a segment exceeding 1000 spans or validates eviction/root-span-retention behavior, so this edge case is unverified.

Redirect-chain loop bound silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing the explanatory warning comment

The loop that follows redirect pointers (`for i = 0, 1000 do ... end`) was previously bounded at 10000 with a comment explaining that 'segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' The bound was cut to 1000 and the comment was deleted entirely. This makes it 10x more likely that deep redirect/segment trees fail to be joined correctly, and removes the only documentation warning future maintainers about this trade-off, with no corresponding test for deep trees near/above the new limit.

Shared BasePaginator.get_result silently clamps negative offsets instead of erroring, affecting all cursor paginators

`BasePaginator.get_result` (used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and now `OptimizedCursorPaginator` — i.e. most cursor-paginated endpoints in the codebase) used to do `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` directly. The change introduces `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which silently clamps negative offsets to 0 for non-prev cursors instead of letting the previous (implicit) error surface. This changes pagination semantics for every endpoint built on `BasePaginator`, not just the audit log endpoint this PR is nominally about, and ships with no new/updated tests demonstrating the previous vs. new behavior across those call sites.

Unconditional dict indexing on end_timestamp_precise can crash the consumer on payloads missing the field

`process_batch` now does `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` via direct key access with no fallback, where `val` is the raw span payload deserialized from Kafka. If any ingested message lacks this field (e.g. during a rollout where Relay has not yet started populating it everywhere, replay of older backlog messages, or a malformed/older-schema payload), this raises `KeyError` and will crash/raise inside the batch-processing task, taking down the whole consumer batch rather than degrading gracefully. Given this is a critical ingestion pipeline, a schema-evolution-safe default (e.g. `.get('end_timestamp_precise', ...)`) or explicit validation should be used instead of hard failure.

max_segment_spans constructor parameter is now dead code; segment size cap is a hardcoded magic number in Lua, decoupled from configuration

`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but the Python-side enforcement of this limit in `_load_segment_data` was removed entirely in this PR. The new eviction cap is hardcoded as the literal `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua` (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', ...)`), completely independent of `self.max_segment_spans`. Callers who construct `SpansBuffer` with a custom `max_segment_spans` value will silently get no effect from that setting, which is a misleading public API and an operational trap for anyone trying to tune this value.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. `cache_key = f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` uses the built-in `hash()` to fold the sorted project id tuple into the cache key. Distinct sets of project ids can map to the same hash value (hash collisions), which would cause the eligibility decision computed for one set of projects to be served from cache for a different, unrelated set of projects sharing the same organization id, within the 60s TTL. A deterministic, collision-resistant encoding (e.g. a delimited string of sorted ids) should be used instead of relying on `hash()`, which is also not part of any stable contract for this purpose.

If that holds here, comparing a seconds-based error timestamp against millisecond-based event timestamps will produce badly out-of-order interleaving (errors will appear to occur either far before or far after all breadcrumbs). However, when matching the user-supplied code here (`credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")`) and in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts (`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")`), no case normalization (e.g. `.toLowerCase()`) is applied before the `indexOf` comparison. true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code validation has a read-then-write race condition allowing double use

In the credentials authorize() handler, a backup code is validated by decrypting `user.backupCodes`, finding the matching index (`backupCodes.indexOf(...)`), and only afterwards persisting the invalidated code back to the DB (`backupCodes[index] = null` followed by `prisma.user.update`). There is no transaction, row lock, or atomic conditional update between the read and the write. Two concurrent login attempts (or an attacker replaying a captured request) using the same backup code can both read the un-invalidated code, both pass validation, and both succeed in logging in before either write completes — violating the single-use guarantee that backup codes are supposed to provide. This should use an atomic update (e.g. a conditional update keyed on the still-encrypted blob, or a per-code DB row with a unique/used flag) instead of decrypt → compute in memory → re-encrypt → write.

Backup-codes download Blob URL is never revoked when the modal is cancelled, leaking memory

`handleSetup` creates a Blob URL via `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` and stores it in `backupCodesUrl`. Backup code request field is used without type/presence validation before calling string methods

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes `req.body.backupCode` is always a string whenever it is truthy, but request bodies from an API endpoint are not type-checked. Backup codes only ever need an equality check to be verified (unlike the TOTP secret, which must be decrypted repeatedly to compute codes). Using a one-way hash would reduce the blast radius of a database/key compromise for this specific secret.

The new string `"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` is shown when a user's `backupCodes` column is null but 2FA is otherwise enabled. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inverted condition for setting organization slug breaks org creation

The condition for assigning `slug` was changed from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the logic. Combined with the unchanged `requestedSlug` assignment (`...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { requestedSlug: slug } : {})`), when billing is disabled the newly created organization now gets neither `slug` nor `requestedSlug`, so the org has no usable slug at all; when billing is enabled it gets both `slug` and a pending `requestedSlug`, which is contradictory. This change is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (destinationCalendar handling) and looks like an accidental regression from a bad merge/rebase that will break organization creation, particularly for self-hosted instances where billing is disabled.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Error logging removed from updateAllCalendarEvents failure path

The previous `console.error(message)` call in the catch block of `updateAllCalendarEvents` was removed when converting the single-reference return to the multi-reference `.map()` version. Errors that occur while updating calendar events (e.g. missing credentials) are now silently swallowed without any log output, making production issues in this path much harder to diagnose.

Hangout link patch call omits the "primary" fallback used for insert

In `createEvent`, the `calendar.events.insert` call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the subsequent `calendar.events.patch` call (to attach the hangout link in the description) uses the raw `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the same fallback. If no destinationCalendar entry matches the current `credentialId` (so `selectedCalendar` is `undefined`), the insert succeeds against "primary" but the patch call is made with an undefined calendarId, which will fail to update the description with the hangout link.

Inconsistent null vs empty-array representation of "no destination calendar" across code paths

This test now expects `destinationCalendar: []` for the BOOKING_REJECTED webhook payload (produced via confirm.handler.ts, which always falls back to `[]`), while the BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED tests in the same file still expect `destinationCalendar: null` (produced via handleNewBooking.ts, which falls back to `null`). Both represent the same "no calendar connected" state but surface differently depending on which code path produced the CalendarEvent. Since `destinationCalendar` is now a public/typed field consumed by webhooks and third-party integrations, this inconsistency (`null` in some flows, `[]` in others) is a fragile and confusing contract that should be normalized to one representation.

No tests cover multi-host destinationCalendar behavior introduced by this PR

This PR converts `destinationCalendar` from a single object to an array across 22 files and rewrites significant parts of EventManager.ts, CalendarManager.ts, and handleNewBooking.ts's collective-event calendar logic (including the host-list building at this line and the `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)` call), but the author's checklist explicitly states no tests were added, and the only test file touched (webhook.e2e.ts) merely adjusts one assertion to match the new shape rather than verifying the multi-host calendar invite behavior described as the purpose of the PR. Given the number of latent bugs this refactor introduces (e.g. the no-op push when destinationCalendar is null, and the Google Calendar organizer-override/fallback bugs), the lack of any automated test for the actual collective multi-host calendar scenario is a significant gap for a change of this risk level.

Organizer email override always uses the first destinationCalendar regardless of which host's credential is creating the event

`mainHostDestinationCalendar` is destructured as the first element of `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar` and used to override the organizer attendee's email (`email: mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId ? mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId : calEventRaw.organizer.email`). When `createAllCalendarEvents` loops over multiple destination calendars/hosts and calls `createEvent` once per host credential, every call still uses the same first-array-entry override instead of the entry matching the `credentialId` actually creating the event (which is correctly looked up a few lines later via `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)`). As a result, for collective events with multiple hosts, every secondary host's calendar event will show the first host's calendar email as the "organizer" attendee instead of their own, undermining the core fix this PR is meant to deliver. The same bug exists in `updateEvent` (lines 198-230) with `mainHostDestinationCalendar`.

Pushing team destination calendars onto evt.destinationCalendar is a no-op when it is null

`destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists (see the ternary ending in `: null,`). Later, `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars);` uses optional chaining, which silently does nothing when `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null`. Consequently, for a COLLECTIVE event where the organizer has no personal destination calendar but other hosts do, all the collected `teamDestinationCalendars` are discarded and only the organizer is considered (incorrectly, with none at all), so secondary hosts never get their calendar invites created — defeating the main goal of this PR in exactly the scenario it is meant to fix.

Same dead fallback logic duplicated in deleteEvent

`const calendarId = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` has the identical self-referential bug as in updateEvent: the `.find` predicate compares against the already-known-falsy `externalCalendarId`, so it never matches and always yields `undefined`. Unlike updateEvent, this one is masked by the subsequent `calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` fallback to `"primary"`, but it means the code silently falls back to deleting from the primary calendar instead of the correct destination calendar whenever `externalCalendarId` is not supplied, which can delete the wrong event or fail to delete the intended one for secondary host calendars.

organization.slug selection dropped from loadUsers query for dynamic bookings

In the refactored `loadUsers` function, the Prisma `select` used for the dynamic/group booking branch (`!eventTypeId`) no longer includes `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, which was present before this change. If any downstream code in this handler (or in dynamic booking flows generally) relies on `organizerUser.organization?.slug` (e.g., for organization-aware booking links), it will now silently receive `undefined`, changing behavior for dynamic/group bookings tied to an organization without any related test coverage added.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback overwrites real refresh_token with the literal string "refresh_token"

When `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` is falsy (e.g. because the schema stripped it, or because the provider legitimately omits refresh_token on refresh responses - several providers, including Office365 whose schema marks `refresh_token` as optional, do not always return a new refresh_token), this code assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"` as the refresh token value. That bogus placeholder then gets persisted to the credential's `key` in the database, permanently destroying the real refresh token and breaking all subsequent token refreshes for that credential until the user re-authenticates. This can happen even without the new credential-sync feature enabled, as a regression for any provider whose refresh endpoint omits refresh_token.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema uses broken computed property keys, stripping all fields except access_token

The schema is built with `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. Calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema instance does not produce a dynamic/catch-all key based on the input data - it returns a fixed literal string (effectively the default `Object.prototype.toString()` output, the same value for both computed keys). The resulting zod object schema therefore only actually validates `access_token` plus one bogus, never-matching literal key. Because `z.object()` strips unknown keys by default (no `.passthrough()`), every other field in the token response (`expiry_date`, `refresh_token`, `expires_in`, etc.) is silently dropped from the parsed result whenever the minimum schema is used (i.e. whenever `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set). This corrupts the stored credential object (fields are lost) and, combined with the refresh_token fallback a few lines below, actively destroys real refresh tokens, breaking the very feature this PR implements.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync-endpoint response shape does not match what several callers expect, causing runtime failures

When credential sync is enabled, this function returns the raw, un-parsed `fetch` `Response` object from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. However several callers assume a different shape depending on their normal (non-sync) refresh implementation: GoogleCalendarService reads `res?.data` (expecting an axios/googleapis-style response), HubspotCalendarService reads properties like `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` directly off the return value (expecting an already-parsed `HubspotToken` object), and the Zoho-Bigin/ZohoCRM CalendarServices read `tokenInfo.data` (expecting an axios response). None of these properties exist on a raw fetch `Response`, so when sync mode is enabled these integrations will silently receive `undefined` values (NaN expiry dates, undefined access tokens) or throw, and then typically fail to persist anything useful, breaking token refresh for these providers under the very feature this PR adds.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

None of these properties exist on a raw fetch `Response`, so when sync mode is enabled these integrations will silently receive `undefined` values (NaN expiry dates, undefined access tokens) or throw, and then typically fail to persist anything useful, breaking token refresh for these providers under the very feature this PR adds.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unvalidated request body/decryption can throw unhandled exceptions

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` uses `.parse` (which throws on invalid input) instead of `.safeParse`, and there is no try/catch around it or around `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` further down. A malformed request body or payload that fails decryption/JSON parsing will throw an uncaught exception inside the handler instead of returning a controlled 400 response, and the handler also never checks `req.method`, so non-POST requests are processed the same way.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Credential lookup via findFirst can target the wrong credential when multiple exist for the same app/user

The handler finds an existing credential with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and, if found, overwrites its `key`. Several apps (e.g. Google Calendar) support installing multiple credentials of the same type for one user. `findFirst` with no explicit ordering can return any one of them non-deterministically, so this sync could silently overwrite the wrong one of a user's multiple connected accounts for the same app.

Outgoing credential-sync request has no HTTP status check and no built-in authentication

The POST request made to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` carries no authentication header/secret from Cal.com's side (only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body), and the response is returned and used regardless of `response.ok`. A failing or malicious response at this endpoint (e.g. a 4xx/5xx or an endpoint that answers unauthenticated) would be treated as a successful token refresh, and the self-hosted receiving endpoint has no way to verify the request actually originated from the paired Cal.com deployment, since no shared secret is sent.

Salesforce token refresh was not wired up to the new credential-sync mechanism

Unlike every other provider touched by this PR (Google Calendar, Office365, Hubspot, Zoom, Webex, Lark, Zoho CRM/Bigin), the newly added Salesforce refresh-token logic calls `fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token", ...)` directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`. As a result, enabling `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`/`CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no effect for Salesforce credentials; they will always be refreshed against Salesforce directly, contradicting the PR's stated goal of letting self-hosters' app store be the source of truth for all apps, and nothing in the PR description calls out this exclusion.

Unrelated change replaces dynamic redirect URI with a hardcoded slug

This line was changed from `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback\`` to the hardcoded `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback\``. This is unrelated to the credential-sync feature described in the PR, and it introduces maintenance drift risk: if `appConfig.slug` in `config.json` is ever updated, this redirect URI will silently stop matching the app's configured slug, instead of automatically staying in sync.

Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time

The webhook secret check uses plain `!==` string comparison between the request header and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This is vulnerable to timing attacks that could help an attacker brute-force the secret byte-by-byte. Given that a correct secret grants the ability to create/overwrite arbitrary users' third-party credentials (full account/app takeover), this comparison should use a constant-time equality check (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`).

appStoreMetadata is looked up by app.slug, but the generated metadata map is keyed by app directory name, not slug

`appStoreMetadata` is generated by scanning app-store directories and is keyed by each app's folder/dirName (e.g. `office365video`, `googlecalendar`, `zoomvideo`, `larkcalendar`), while `app.slug` (and `reqBody.appSlug`) is the user-facing slug stored on the `App` model, which frequently differs from the directory name (e.g. slug `msteams` for dir `office365video`, slug `google-calendar` for dir `googlecalendar`, slug `zoom` for dir `zoomvideo`, slug `lark-calendar` for dir `larkcalendar`). Indexing `appStoreMetadata` with `app.slug` will return `undefined` for most of these apps, causing the handler to incorrectly respond with 404 "App not found" even though the app and slug are valid, breaking credential sync for the majority of the apps this PR claims to support.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest email blacklist comparison is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass

`blacklistedGuestEmails` is built by lower-casing every entry from `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS`, but the comparison `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` uses the raw, non-lowercased `guest` value. A blocked email such as `spam@example.com` can bypass the blacklist simply by submitting `Spam@Example.com` or `SPAM@EXAMPLE.COM`, since the exact-case string will never match the lowercased blacklist entries.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner permission check uses AND instead of OR

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. Since `isTeamOwner` is a strict subset of `isTeamAdmin` (an OWNER role satisfies both, but an ADMIN-only role satisfies only `isTeamAdmin`), this expression is effectively equivalent to just `isTeamOwner`. As a result, a team ADMIN who is not also the OWNER, and who is neither the booking organizer nor an attendee, will be incorrectly denied with FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests to a team member's booking, even though team admins should normally have this privilege (as elsewhere in the codebase, e.g. reassign). This should be `||`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Wrong attendee email template sent when a resubmitted guest email is not actually new

`sendAddGuestsEmails(calEvent, newGuests)` decides which template to send an attendee based on `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`. The caller (`addGuests.handler.ts`, line 168) passes the raw, unfiltered `guests` array from the request rather than `uniqueGuests` (the guests that were actually inserted after filtering out existing attendees and blacklisted emails). If a user resubmits an email that is already an existing attendee (so it gets filtered out of `uniqueGuests` and not re-added to the DB), that existing attendee's email is still present in `guests`, causing them to incorrectly receive the full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (meant for brand-new attendees) instead of `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`, which is confusing and semantically wrong.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_positives.candidate:
Duplicate-guest detection is case-sensitive

`uniqueGuests` is derived by checking `guest === attendee.email` without normalizing case. Combined with the client-side uniqueness check in AddGuestsDialog.tsx (which also does a case-sensitive `Set` comparison), a guest can be added twice with differing email casing (e.g. `John@Example.com` vs `john@example.com`), creating duplicate Attendee rows that represent the same real email address and causing duplicate notifications/calendar invites for what is effectively the same guest.

Email-send failure is swallowed with a bare console.log, losing error details

The `catch (err)` block around `sendAddGuestsEmails` only logs the static string `"Error sending AddGuestsEmails"` via `console.log`, discarding the actual `err` object and bypassing the project's structured logger (`@calcom/lib/logger`) used elsewhere in this same file's imports. This makes it impossible to diagnose production email failures for this flow, and `console.log` (rather than `console.error`/the logger) is inconsistent with how errors are handled elsewhere in the codebase.

EventManager built with requesting user's credentials instead of the booking organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` fetches credentials for the user making the request, and `EventManager` is instantiated with `{ ...user, credentials }` where `user` is `ctx.user`. Because the permission check above allows an attendee (not just the organizer) to add guests, when an attendee triggers this flow the calendar sync in `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` will run with the attendee's own (likely absent or unrelated) calendar credentials rather than the organizer's. The booking already fetched `user: { include: { destinationCalendar: true, credentials: true } }` (the organizer), but those credentials are never used. This can silently fail to update the organizer's actual calendar event with the new guests.

Fallback toast message in onError is dead code

`showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error")` uses `message` which is built from a template literal (`` `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}` ``) and is therefore always a non-empty, truthy string even when `err.data` or `err.message` are undefined (yielding something like "undefined: undefined"). The `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback can never actually trigger, so users may see a raw/unhelpful "undefined: ..." message instead of the intended friendly error text for unexpected error shapes.

Hardcoded, non-localized tooltip text

The remove-email tooltip uses a hardcoded English string `<Tooltip content="Remove email">` instead of going through the `t()` translation function that is already imported and used elsewhere in this same component (e.g. for "add_another" and the field label). This breaks localization for non-English users of this new shared UI component.

No automated tests for the new add-guests feature

This PR introduces a new tRPC mutation with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer/attendee/team-admin checks), guest deduplication/blacklist filtering, calendar sync, and dual email notifications, plus new UI components (`AddGuestsDialog`, `MultiEmail`). No unit, integration, or component tests are included for any of `addGuests.handler.ts`, `addGuests.schema.ts`, `AddGuestsDialog.tsx`, or `MultiEmail.tsx`, despite the permission-check bug and case-sensitivity issues that tests would likely have caught.

No check on booking status before adding guests

The handler fetches the booking and immediately proceeds to add attendees, sync the calendar and send notification emails without verifying `booking.status`. Guests can therefore be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings, resulting in calendar invites and "guests added" notification emails being sent for an event that is not actually happening, confusing invitees and polluting calendars with stale events.

isInvalidEmail state is never reset after a successful submission or new attempt

`isInvalidEmail` is only reset to `false` in the Cancel button handler. If a user triggers the "emails must be unique and valid" error once, then fixes the input and successfully submits (via `handleAdd`'s success branch or the mutation's `onSuccess`), `isInvalidEmail` remains `true`. Since the dialog closes on success but the flag is never cleared, reopening the dialog afterward will immediately show the stale invalid-email warning banner even though no new validation error has occurred.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount increment is not atomic, risking lost updates under overlapping cron runs

Both the failure branch (lines 178-187) and the catch block (lines 190-197) compute the new retryCount as `reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value fetched once at the start of the request, then write it back. If the cron endpoint is invoked again before the previous invocation finishes (e.g., due to a slow run or concurrent triggers), two overlapping runs could both read the same stale retryCount and write the same incremented value, effectively losing an increment. Using Prisma's atomic `{ retryCount: { increment: 1 } }` would avoid this race and guarantee failures are counted correctly regardless of overlap.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany retryCount branch is not scoped to method: SMS

In the deleteMany() call (lines 29-45), the OR clause's second condition `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` constraint, unlike the first condition which explicitly filters `method: SMS`. Since `retryCount` was added as a shared column on the `WorkflowReminder` model (used by all methods: EMAIL, SMS, WHATSAPP), this query will delete ANY workflow reminder (regardless of method) whose retryCount happens to exceed 1, not just SMS reminders. Today only this file increments retryCount so it only affects SMS reminders in practice, but the query itself is inconsistent with the stated purpose (cleaning up SMS reminders) and is a latent bug waiting to silently delete Email/WhatsApp reminders if retryCount is ever incremented elsewhere.

false_positives.candidate:
New retryCount update inside catch block can throw and abort processing of remaining reminders

The catch block (lines 189-199) now performs an additional `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` with no surrounding try/catch. If this update itself fails (e.g., the record was concurrently deleted by the deleteMany cleanup on a parallel/overlapping cron invocation, a transient DB error, etc.), the exception propagates out of the `for` loop entirely since nothing catches it there. This means a single failure updating one reminder's retryCount aborts processing of all subsequent reminders in the batch for that cron invocation, and likely results in an unhandled promise rejection / 500 response instead of the previous behavior where errors were only logged and the loop continued. This is a regression in robustness for a cron job meant to process many independent reminders.

No test coverage added for new retryCount/deletion behavior

This PR introduces non-trivial new logic (incrementing retryCount on failure, and deleting reminders after retryCount exceeds the threshold) but adds no unit or integration tests to verify: (1) retryCount is incremented correctly on twilio.scheduleSMS failure and on thrown errors, (2) reminders are deleted once retryCount surpasses the threshold, and (3) the deleteMany query only targets the intended records. Given the subtlety of the query logic (see the unscoped retryCount deletion condition), tests would have caught at least one of the issues introduced here.

Reminders with no sendTo/message never get retryCount incremented, leaving them stuck indefinitely

The retryCount increment logic only runs inside the `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` block (success/failure) or inside the catch block. If `sendTo` is empty/undefined or `message` resolves to an empty string (e.g., attendee has no SMS number, or reminderBody/template produced no text), this whole block is skipped silently — no error is thrown, no retryCount increment happens. Such reminders will remain `scheduled: false` and keep getting re-selected and reprocessed by every cron run until their `scheduledDate` passes, without ever reaching the retryCount threshold that this PR introduces to stop infinite retries. This defeats the stated goal of the PR for one of the most common real failure causes (missing/invalid phone number resulting in an empty sendTo rather than a thrown error).

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unreachable fallback branches in getBaseConditions due to buildAuthorizationConditions never returning falsy

`getBaseConditions()` branches on `if (authConditions && filterConditions) ... else if (authConditions) ... else if (filterConditions) ... else return NOTHING_CONDITION`. However `buildAuthorizationConditions()` (and thus `getAuthorizationConditions()`) always returns a `Prisma.Sql` object (never null/undefined), so `authConditions` is always truthy. The `else if (filterConditions)` and final `else` branches are therefore dead code that can mask a future contract change (e.g. if `getAuthorizationConditions` is later made to return null in some case, the fallback behavior silently differs from what a reader would expect).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching behavior tests were deleted instead of updated

The previous test suite included a `describe("Caching", ...)` block with two tests ("should cache authorization conditions" and "should cache filter conditions") that verified `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` caching logic. Consequently `end > workingHour.endTime` is equivalent to re-checking `start > workingHour.endTime`, so a slot that starts within business hours but whose duration would push it past the host's configured closing time is never flagged as out of bounds.
