true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two separately-created Dayjs object instances with reference equality. Two different `dayjs()` calls never return the same object reference, so this condition is always `false`, even when the override truly has start === end (the common representation of a date override that blocks an entire day). Because this branch is unreachable, a date override meant to mark a whole day unavailable for a fixed host/organizer will not be detected here, and the slot can still be considered available — directly undermining the goal of this PR (respecting fixed-host date overrides).

false_positives.candidate:
No automated test for the headline round-robin fixed-host date-override fix

The PR description states its primary goal is to ensure round-robin events respect a fixed host's date overrides so slots aren't offered when the fixed host is unavailable. The only tests added ('Check for Date overrides' and its new timezone variant) use a single-user event type with `hosts: []` and no `schedulingType`, so they never exercise the `fixedHosts`/`isFixed` branch together with a `ROUND_ROBIN` schedulingType and a date override. There is no regression test creating a round-robin event with a fixed host that has a date override, verifying that slots outside that override are excluded while the round-robin (non-fixed) host's own availability does not override it — the exact scenario this PR claims to fix.

Working-hours check never flags a day the host has no entries for at all

The `workingHours.find((workingHour) => { if (workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())) {...} })` guard at lines 139-148 only evaluates the out-of-range condition for workingHours entries whose `days` already include the slot's weekday. If a fixed host has no workingHours entry at all for that weekday (i.e. a day off with zero availability rows), none of the entries ever return `true`, `.find()` returns `undefined`, and the surrounding `if` is skipped entirely — the function falls through to the busy-time check instead of returning `false`. As a result, a fixed host who simply does not work on a given day is still treated as available for that day as long as there is no conflicting busy time. This is exactly the scenario this PR claims to fix for round-robin events (slots should not be offered when the fixed host is unavailable), so this logic gap leaves the core bug only partially fixed.

`dateOverrides.find()` short-circuits on the first same-day override, breaking multi-range overrides

The availability decision for date overrides (lines 106-131) is based on the first override entry whose date matches the slot's date, via `Array.prototype.find`. If a user has more than one override time range configured for the same calendar date (e.g. a split day with a morning and an afternoon range), and the slot falls within the second range but not the first, the first entry's callback already sets `dateOverrideExist = true` and returns `true` (since `slotStartTime.isAfter(dayjs(date.end)...)` for the earlier range), causing `.find()` to stop and the outer `if` to return `false` (unavailable) for a slot that is actually covered by the later range. This produces incorrect 'unavailable' results whenever a date has multiple override ranges.

`timeZone` added as optional but is now functionally required for correct override math

`TimeRange.timeZone` was added as an optional field, yet `packages/lib/slots.ts` now relies on it (`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)`) to compute the organizer's UTC offset for a date override. Nothing in the type enforces that every caller supplies it; if a `DateOverride`/`TimeRange` is constructed without `timeZone` (e.g. by another call site not updated in this PR), `dayjs(...).tz(undefined)` silently falls back to the dayjs-timezone plugin's 'guess' (the server process's local timezone) instead of erroring, which would silently produce incorrect slot times rather than surfacing the missing data.

`queued` datetime is not safely round-tripped through task serialization

`to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which keeps `queued` as a raw `datetime` object. This dict is passed verbatim as Celery task kwargs (`assignment_source_dict`) in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (`src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py`). If the task broker uses JSON serialization, the `datetime` will be converted to an ISO string on the wire, but `AssignmentSource.from_dict()` (line 30-35) does not convert it back into a `datetime` when reconstructing the object — it just passes the raw dict through `cls(**input_dict)`. This leaves `queued` as a `str` on the consumer side instead of the declared `datetime` type, which can raise exceptions or silently misbehave wherever `queued` is later treated as a datetime. No test exercises the actual serialize/deserialize round trip through the task boundary, so this discrepancy is not caught.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op due to earlier global monkeypatch, defeating its purpose

The test patches the global `time.sleep` with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` call (with comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change') therefore also resolves to the same no-op lambda, since monkeypatch replaces the attribute on the shared `time` module used by both the test and the flusher's background thread. The intended 100ms wall-clock wait never happens, so the test's correctness now relies on incidental GIL/thread-scheduling timing rather than a deterministic wait, which can make the test flaky under CI load despite the comment implying a real wait was added to fix flakiness.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can skip terminate() for multiple flusher subprocesses on timeout

In join(), the per-process loop does `if deadline is not None: remaining_time = deadline - time.time(); if remaining_time <= 0: break`. Once the overall deadline has elapsed (e.g. because an earlier process took a while to die, or next_step.join(timeout) already consumed most of the timeout), the loop breaks immediately for that process and all subsequent processes in `self.processes`, so `process.terminate()` (line 346-347) is never called for them. In the old single-process implementation, terminate() was called unconditionally after the wait loop regardless of the deadline. Now, with multiple flusher processes, a timed-out join() can leave one or more child processes running and un-terminated after join() returns (e.g. during partition rebalance), potentially continuing to read Redis and produce segments for shards the consumer no longer owns, which can cause duplicate/late segment production to Kafka and resource leaks.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

false_positives.candidate:
New multiprocess test only checks shard→process bookkeeping, not actual flush behavior

This leaves the core new feature of this PR — correct end-to-end flushing when more than one flusher process/thread is active — without a test that exercises actual data flow and verifies correctness across multiple processes.

Unused dead code: `_create_process_for_shard`

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` (singular) is defined but never called anywhere in the class; all restart paths (`_ensure_processes_alive`) call `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) directly with the process_index and full shard list. This leftover method suggests an incomplete refactor (e.g. an intended per-shard-only restart path that was dropped) and should either be wired up or removed to avoid confusing maintainers.

`max_processes or len(...)` silently discards an explicit 0, and CLI option allows invalid values

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses `or`, so an explicitly passed `max_processes=0` is treated the same as `None` and silently replaced by one-process-per-shard instead of being honored or rejected. Additionally, the new `--flusher-processes` click option in src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py (around lines 432-437) has no `min=1` validation, so a negative value causes `self.num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards))` to become negative; `range(negative_number)` yields an empty dict for `process_to_shards_map`, and the subsequent `self.process_to_shards_map[process_index].append(shard)` assignment then raises an unhandled `KeyError` at consumer startup rather than a clear configuration error.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling assertion is racy and contradicts the test's stated intent

The test's docstring states it verifies "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages," implying the successfully-processed message's offset should still get committed. However the final assertion is `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which actually asserts that NO commit happened. Since `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` completes (and thus makes committable) an offset in its `finally` block regardless of whether `result_processor` raised, both offsets (100 and 101) should become contiguous and committable once both items are processed, and the asynchronous commit loop (`_commit_loop`, firing every 1 second) will eventually commit offset 102. The test's wait loop (max ~0.2-2.2s) races against that 1-second commit cycle: on a fast run the assertion passes merely because the periodic commit hasn't fired yet, not because the intended behavior holds, and on a slower CI run (where the loop takes closer to its 2s budget) the commit may already have happened, making the test flaky/liable to fail intermittently. The assertion does not reliably validate the described behavior either way.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
CLI help text for --mode not updated to describe the new thread-queue-parallel mode

The `--mode` option's choices were extended to include `thread-queue-parallel` (line 121), but the help string still reads "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." (line 123), which does not mention or explain the new mode's semantics (fixed queue pool with per-group ordering guarantees). Operators using `--help` to choose a processing mode have no way to understand what thread-queue-parallel does or how it differs from parallel/batched-parallel.

Internal queues have no maxsize, so the advertised "natural backpressure" does not exist

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring (around line 253) claims the strategy provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but each per-group queue is constructed as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (line 185), which defaults to an unbounded queue. `put()` therefore never blocks, so there is no backpressure mechanism at all: if one hashed queue backs up (exactly the scenario this PR is meant to mitigate), the consumer will keep reading from Kafka and enqueueing work indefinitely, growing memory without bound instead of slowing down. This contradicts the documented guarantee and creates an OOM risk under the very failure mode the PR targets.

Use of queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown() requires Python 3.13+

This module relies on `queue.ShutDown` (lines 132, 142) and `queue.Queue.shutdown()` (line 238, called from FixedQueuePool.shutdown at lines 231-243), both of which were only added to the standard library in Python 3.13. If Sentry's runtime is on an earlier Python version (3.11/3.12, which has been the case historically for this codebase), referencing `queue.ShutDown` or calling `.shutdown()` on a `queue.Queue` instance will raise `AttributeError` at runtime, crashing the consumer during normal strategy shutdown/rebalance/termination paths (i.e. the thread-queue-parallel mode would be completely non-functional, not just degraded).

close()/terminate() permanently destroy the factory-level shared FixedQueuePool, breaking subsequent Kafka rebalances

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (result_consumer.py lines 131-137) and is meant to live for the lifetime of the factory, the same way `self.multiprocessing_pool` and `self.parallel_executor` do (those are only torn down in `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()`, never by a per-assignment strategy). However, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (line 338) and `.terminate()` (line 342) call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` directly, which permanently calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every internal queue and stops every worker thread in the shared pool. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the currently active strategy and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again on the *same factory instance* on every partition rebalance (not just final consumer shutdown). After the very first rebalance, the shared `queue_pool` is dead: its queues are shut down and its worker threads have exited, but `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` in result_consumer.py (lines 244-259) just reuses `self.queue_pool` without recreating it. Any subsequent `submit()` call on the new strategy will raise `queue.ShutDown` from `work_queue.put()`, which is caught by the generic `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`; that handler then marks the offset as added+completed as if it were processed, even though the message was never passed to `result_processor`. This causes silent data loss for every message after the first rebalance while still advancing committed offsets, defeating the purpose of the feature and corrupting data integrity guarantees.

join(timeout) ignores the timeout argument and duplicates close() shutdown logic

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout=None)` (line 345) simply calls `self.close()`, discarding the caller-provided `timeout`. Arroyo's `ProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` contract is expected to block up to the given timeout waiting for outstanding work to flush before shutdown completes; here the actual draining/joining logic in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (lines 231-243) hardcodes a fixed 5.0 second timeout for both queue draining and worker-thread joins, regardless of what timeout the stream processor configured for graceful shutdown (e.g. `join_timeout` passed through `get_stream_processor`). This can cause premature strategy teardown if more time was actually available, and if `close()` is invoked followed by `join()` (both call the same shutdown path), the second invocation triggers `queue_pool.shutdown()` again on already-shutdown queues, causing extra "Error shutting down queue" exception logs on every normal shutdown.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New denial-cache test doesn't actually verify the denial-cache short-circuit

In TestService_CacheCheck's 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' subtest, the comment claims 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked', but the permCache entry is set to `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` (an explicit false) rather than `true`. Since reading a missing key or an explicit false both yield `false` from a Go map, and `s.store`/`s.permissionStore`/`s.folderStore` are left as the default empty fakeStore (which returns no permissions and no folders without error), the test would still produce `Allowed: false` via the normal fallback path even if the permDenialCache short-circuit were broken or removed entirely. The test therefore provides no real coverage of the new denial-cache behavior it is supposed to validate.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
userPermDenialCacheKey is vulnerable to key collisions because its fields are joined with '_' without escaping

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name and parent with a plain '_' delimiter: `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Grafana dashboard/folder UIDs are allowed to contain underscores (UID validation permits [a-zA-Z0-9_-]+), so two different (action, name, parent) triples can produce the identical cache key string (e.g. action='A', name='B_C', parent='D' vs action='A_B', name='C', parent='D' both yield '..._A_B_C_D'). Because every denial-cache entry stores the same value (`true`), a collision causes a denial cached for one resource/action to be incorrectly served as a cached denial for a completely unrelated resource/action belonging to the same user, wrongly blocking access that was never actually evaluated, for up to the cache TTL.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache can reintroduce the exact staleness bug this PR is meant to fix

The new permission-denial cache (checked at lines 116-121 and populated at line 154) is consulted before the regular permission cache or any DB fallback, and has the same 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) as the rest of the caches. Once a Check() call for a specific (namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder) combination is denied, every subsequent Check() for that exact resource short-circuits to `Allowed: false` for up to 30 seconds, with no invalidation hook tied to permission grants/role/team changes. If a user is denied access to a resource and is then granted access (e.g. shared a dashboard, added to a team, or the permission write for a just-created resource lands slightly after the first check), the user will continue to be denied for up to 30 seconds even though a fresh DB query would now return 'allowed'. This reproduces, for the negative-cache case, the same 'cannot access what I should now have access to' symptom that this PR is otherwise trying to fix by falling back to the DB on cache misses.

Denial-cache hits and permission-cache hits are reported under the same metric labels

In Check(), both a denial-cache hit (line 118) and a positive permission-cache hit (around line 132) increment `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action)`. These are two distinct caches (permDenialCache vs permCache) with different semantics and TT悠L behavior, but the metric conflates them into a single 'cache hit' counter per action. This makes it impossible to measure the effectiveness/behavior of each cache independently from metrics, reducing the observability value that this feature is supposed to add.

List() does not get the same freshness fallback as Check(), so newly created/newly granted resources may still be missing from list results

Check() was changed so that when the cached permission map doesn't grant the specific requested resource, it falls back to a fresh DB query (fixing the 'can't access what I just created' bug for single-resource checks). List(), however, only distinguishes cache-hit vs cache-miss as a whole (lines 180-192): if `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns any cached map at all, that stale map is used as-is to build the list, with no mechanism to detect that it is missing a newly created/newly granted item. As a result, a user who creates a dashboard/folder may be able to directly Check() access to it immediately (via the DB fallback), but the item can still be absent from List() results (e.g. folder/dashboard browse views) for up to shortCacheTTL (30s), partially undermining the stated goal of letting creators see resources they just created.

Removing the client-side cache entirely for in-proc mode increases per-check overhead

The in-proc AccessClient is now constructed with `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})` instead of a real local cache, meaning every single Check/List call from any in-proc caller must always traverse request validation, the in-proc gRPC channel/interceptor, and the server-side cache lookups, instead of being able to short-circuit via a cheap client-side memory lookup as before. For call patterns that issue many repeated/duplicate permission checks in quick succession (e.g. rendering a page that checks access on many individual items), this removes a previously-available fast path and could noticeably increase CPU/allocation overhead, even though the server-side caches still avoid the DB round-trip.

Ability hooks are now invoked twice per rule regardless of relevance, doubling permission-check overhead

`AlertRuleMenu` now unconditionally calls both `useRulerRuleAbilities(rulerRule, groupIdentifier, [...])` (lines 57-64) and `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(... , [...])` (lines 67-79) for every rendered rule, even though in the new ruler-less list view `rulerRule` is always `undefined` and the ruler-based branch is a no-op. The Pause menu item (line 123) is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` is true, and the Delete menu item (line 165, `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}`) is only rendered when `rulerRule` is truthy. This silently removes two previously available actions from the alert list's dropdown menu. The regression is masked rather than caught by `GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx`'s 'should render correct menu actions when More button is clicked' test, which grants delete/update permissions yet asserts exactly 4 menu items (Silence, Copy link, Duplicate, Export) with no Delete or Pause entries.

Stale JSDoc still references the Ruler response this component no longer queries

The `expectedRulesCount` prop's doc comment states: "Ruler response might contain different number of rules, but in most cases what we get from Prometheus is fine", implying the component still cross-checks against a ruler response.
