false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Moving interpolation before querySupportsSplitting() defeats the $__range splitting safeguard

querySupportsSplitting() (lines 282-289) relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to detect queries using the $__range family of variables, with the comment explaining that such queries must not be time-split because the interpolated $__range value would otherwise become incorrect. Previously this check ran on the raw (non-interpolated) expr, so the literal '$__range' text was still present and detectable. Now queries are interpolated via datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...) at line 299 before this check runs at line 300, so by the time isQueryWithRangeVariable() executes, any '$__range' reference has already been replaced with its literal value and can no longer be detected in the string. As a result, querySupportsSplitting() can never classify a query as using $__range anymore, so such queries will now flow into the normal time-splitting path (logQueries/metricQueries) instead of being executed as a single non-split request, risking incorrect merged results for queries that depend on $__range spanning the whole original range versus the narrower per-partition sub-ranges. The accompanying comment is now also stale/misleading since the described protection no longer functions as written.

No regression test for $__range queries after reordering interpolation and splitting checks

The PR reorders interpolation to happen before querySupportsSplitting()/isQueryWithRangeVariable() is evaluated (see querySplitting.ts), which changes whether queries using the $__range variable get excluded from time splitting. No test was added (here or elsewhere in this file) that exercises a query containing $__range to confirm it is still correctly excluded from splitting, or to validate the new intended behavior if inclusion is now considered safe. Given this is exactly the kind of interaction the interpolation-timing change affects, its absence leaves a meaningful regression risk unverified.

No test verifies ad hoc filters aren't duplicated due to repeated interpolation

The test 'Interpolates queries before running' now asserts datasource.applyTemplateVariables is called 5 times for a single query (previously the batch call interpolateVariablesInQueries was asserted to run once), confirming the query gets interpolated multiple times across the shard-splitting/time-splitting delegation. None of the tests pass a non-empty request.filters (ad hoc filters) to verify that this repeated interpolation does not duplicate ad hoc filter matchers in the final query selector sent to runQuery. Given applyTemplateVariables is the mechanism typically used to inject ad hoc filters into the query text, and it is now invoked multiple times per logical query, this scenario should be covered by a dedicated test.

Queries get interpolated multiple times when shard splitting delegates to runSplitQuery

runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates every target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters) before any splitting happens (lines 49-53). However, splitQueriesByStreamShard()'s runNextRequest() (shardQuerySplitting.ts, ~line 163) calls runSplitQuery(datasource, subRequest, options) once per shard group/cycle, and runSplitQuery() (querySplitting.ts, lines 296-299) now also unconditionally re-interpolates request.targets via datasource.applyTemplateVariables for every call. Because the sub-request built for each shard group still carries the already-interpolated (and shard-selector-modified) targets, those targets get interpolated again on every shard cycle. This is confirmed by the updated test expectation in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts ('Interpolates queries before running') which changed from `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` to `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` for a single logical query split into 4 shard groups. Repeated interpolation is wasteful, and if applyTemplateVariables is not idempotent (e.g. it injects ad hoc filters as extra label matchers into the selector text, as its own test mock does by mutating query.expr), running it multiple times on the same query risks duplicating ad hoc filter clauses or otherwise corrupting the final selector sent to the backend when ad hoc filters (request.filters) are present.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID field dropped from 'Plugin Request Completed' log line

The previous logRequest implementation in logger_middleware.go explicitly added a "traceID" attribute to the log params via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false). That code (and the tracing import) was removed in this PR, and the replacement contextual-attribute builder here (instrumentContext) only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname - traceID is not restored anywhere. As a result, the 'Plugin Request Completed' log entries emitted by LoggerMiddleware no longer contain a traceID, which is a regression for trace/log correlation that isn't mentioned in the PR description.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards all logger state

TestLogger.FromContext(_ context.Context) returns a brand-new NewTestLogger() instance instead of returning the receiver (or a logger that still writes into the same DebugLogs/InfoLogs/WarnLogs/ErrorLogs fields). Since LoggerMiddleware now always logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)` (see logger_middleware.go), any test using plog.NewTestLogger() to assert on logged messages/calls through code paths that call FromContext will never see those calls recorded on the original TestLogger instance - the call lands on a throwaway logger that is immediately discarded. This makes TestLogger unusable for verifying the new context-aware logging behavior and can mask real bugs in tests that rely on it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to exported Logger interface is a breaking change for other implementers

A new required method, FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger, was added to the exported plugins/log.Logger interface. This PR only updates the two known implementations (grafanaInfraLogWrapper in logger.go and TestLogger in fake.go). Any other type in the codebase (or downstream consumer) that implements plugins/log.Logger without this method will fail to compile/satisfy the interface. This should be verified across the codebase before merging, since interface changes like this silently break unrelated implementers.

Logger name still references old 'instrumentation' naming

clientmiddleware.NewLoggerMiddleware(cfg, log.New("plugin.instrumentation")) still names the logger "plugin.instrumentation" even though this PR's stated purpose is to rename instrumentation-related concepts to metrics-related ones for clarity, and the logger here is purely for request logging (LoggerMiddleware), not metrics. This leaves confusing/incorrect logger naming in production logs after the rename.

No unit test added for new ContextualLoggerMiddleware

This PR introduces a new, independently-registered middleware (ContextualLoggerMiddleware) that carries meaningful logic (building the contextual log attributes from plugin/datasource/user info and depending on being ordered before LoggerMiddleware in the chain). No test file (e.g., contextual_logger_middleware_test.go) was added to verify that the context attributes are correctly set, nor to guard against future middleware-order regressions that would silently break the LoggerMiddleware's enriched logging.

Test function name not updated after rename

The file was renamed from instrumentation_middleware_test.go to metrics_middleware_test.go and the underlying type/constructor were renamed to MetricsMiddleware/newMetricsMiddleware, but the test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware. This leaves a stale, inconsistent name that no longer matches the renamed type or file, contrary to the stated goal of the PR (better naming/consistency).

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race between CountDevices and insert allows exceeding the configured device limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices to check whether the active-device count is >= deviceLimit, and only falls back to updateDevice (reject new devices) when the limit is already reached; otherwise it proceeds with a plain INSERT/UPSERT. There is no transaction, locking, or atomic constraint tying the count check to the subsequent insert. Multiple concurrent requests for different new device IDs can all read a count below the limit and then all insert successfully, letting the active device count exceed deviceLimit. Under any real concurrent anonymous traffic this race defeats the purpose of the configurable device limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit enforcement is bypassed after the first rejection due to caching before persistence succeeds

In tagDeviceUI, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` is executed BEFORE the call to `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice(ctx, device)`. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, which TagDevice now propagates and client.go's Authenticate turns into an authentication failure for that request. However, the cache entry for that device ID was already set during this failed attempt. On the very next request from the same (blocked) device, within the ~29 minute cache TTL, tagDeviceUI short-circuits on `a.localCache.Get(key)` and returns nil without ever calling CreateOrUpdateDevice again. TagDevice then returns nil, and Authenticate proceeds to return a valid anonymous Identity. So after the single first rejection, the same over-the-limit device is silently let through for the remainder of the cache TTL, completely defeating the device limit feature for any device that retries (e.g. a browser reload).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
30-day anonymous-device window duplicated as separate constants across three files

The 30-day 'active device' window is now hardcoded independently in three places: `thirtyDays` in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go (used for usage stats), `anonymousDeviceExpiration` in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore/database.go (used for the device-limit count window and the update-match window), and `anonymousDeviceExpiration` in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/api/api.go (used for listing devices). These must stay numerically identical for the device-limit feature, usage stats, and the devices API to remain consistent; having three independent literals increases the risk that a future change to one location silently desynchronizes the others.

Anonymous authentication now blocks synchronously on a DB call with no timeout, removing previous async/timeout/panic-recovery protections

Previously TagDevice was invoked in a goroutine with its own context.WithTimeout(2*time.Minute) and a recover() to guard against panics, so a slow or failing device-tagging write never affected the latency or stability of the anonymous authentication response. This change removes the goroutine, the timeout, and the panic recovery, and calls `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, httpReqCopy, anonymous.AnonDeviceUI)` synchronously using the request context. Every anonymous authentication for a not-yet-cached device now blocks on a DB upsert (and, when a device limit is configured, an additional COUNT query) with no bounded timeout of its own, and an unrecovered panic in this path would now propagate into the request-handling goroutine. This is a latency and availability regression on the anonymous auth hot path, especially under DB slowness or load.

Changed constructor signature may leave generated DI (Wire) code out of sync

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService's signature changed from accepting `anonStore anonstore.AnonStore` (previously resolved elsewhere, presumably via a Wire provider calling anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore) to accepting `sqlStore db.DB` directly and building the AnonDBStore internally with `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit)`. anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore's own signature also changed (added deviceLimit int64 parameter). The PR's file list does not include any update to generated wire_gen.go (or equivalent DI wiring) that would reference these constructors; if such generated code exists and still calls the old signatures, the build will fail to compile or Wire codegen will fail due to an unused/missing provider. This should be verified and, if needed, regenerated before merge.

New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented

A new ini key `device_limit` under `[auth.anonymous]` is introduced and parsed into `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit`, but the PR does not update conf/defaults.ini (sample config) or the configuration documentation to describe this new setting, its default (0 = unlimited), or its effect. Without this, administrators have no way to discover or understand how to configure the new device limit feature.

No test coverage for cache-bypass or concurrent device-limit races

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a single new device is rejected once the limit is reached; it does not cover (a) that an already-known device can still refresh its timestamp when the limit is reached, (b) concurrent CreateOrUpdateDevice calls for distinct new devices that could race past the limit (see the CountDevices/insert TOCTOU issue), or (c) the interaction between the local cache in impl.go and repeated calls for a device that was previously rejected, which currently lets a rejected device through on retry. These are exactly the scenarios where the new feature is most likely to fail silently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-level logging used for normal/successful cleanup batches, including full ID lists

In CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579), `r.log.Error(...)` is called on every batch iteration even when there is no error. The `err`/`y` values logged at line 534/554/576 are guaranteed nil at that point because the function already returned early on error, so these statements always report a bogus 'error' for a success case. Since these calls run on every batch of every cleanup cycle (now potentially every minute, with batch sizes that can be in the tens of thousands as exercised by the new test), this will flood error-level logs/alerting systems with non-error noise and also logs the entire fetched ID slice (up to the configured batch size) on every iteration, adding unnecessary log volume/overhead. These should be at Debug/Info level and should not include an always-nil error field.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation

The background cleanup ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This affects the entire `clean()` routine, which runs all cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history), not just the annotation cleanup this PR is about. Running every cleanup job 10x more frequently is a significant behavioral/performance change that is not mentioned in the PR description, is unrelated to the stated goal of avoiding MySQL deadlocks (and could actually increase contention since jobs now run far more often), and has no corresponding test coverage or justification. This looks like it may be a leftover debugging change that should be reverted or explicitly justified before merge.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete attaches the wrong logger to the context, losing structured fields

In Delete, `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` builds a logger with contextual fields, but the very next line does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, attaching the base `d.Log` (without the added fields) to the context instead of the local `log` variable. Any code downstream that retrieves the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` (e.g. inside Storage.Delete/Legacy.Delete) will not see the name/kind/method fields, unlike in Create, Update and DeleteCollection which correctly propagate their local `log`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection duration/error is recorded under the storage metric

Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, after calling `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, the result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration`. Every other method (Create, Delete, Update) correctly calls `recordLegacyDuration` for the legacy-side async call; this inconsistency mislabels the Legacy DeleteCollection outcome as a Storage outcome in metrics.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success path records the storage-duration metric with the object name instead of the resource kind

On the success path of Delete, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the per-object `name` as the metric label, whereas the error path two lines above (and every other method in this file) passes `options.Kind`. Using the object's name as a Prometheus label value creates one time series per distinct object name, leading to unbounded metric cardinality and potential monitoring/storage issues in production, in addition to making the metric inconsistent with the error path and with every other method's labeling.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy-write goroutines derive their timeout from a request-scoped context that is likely already canceled

In Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the fire-and-forget goroutine does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` using the *incoming request* ctx as parent. In the real apiserver, `http.Request.Context()` (and the context threaded through REST handlers) is canceled as soon as the handler that invoked Create/Update/Delete returns and the response is written - which happens essentially immediately after the goroutine is spawned, often before the goroutine even runs. Because `context.WithTimeout`/`WithTimeoutCause` on an already-canceled parent returns an already-canceled context, the asynchronous Legacy write will frequently fail immediately with a 'context canceled' error, defeating the entire purpose of mode 3's 'write to legacy as a safety net' feature. This bug is masked in the unit tests because they call the dual writer with `context.Background()`, which never cancels. The goroutines should detach from request cancellation (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` plus a fresh timeout, or `context.Background()` carrying only the needed values) instead of inheriting the request's cancellation.

Storage.Create failure is recorded via recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` (line 45), mislabeling a Storage failure as a Legacy failure. The success path two lines below correctly uses `recordStorageDuration`. This corrupts the error-rate metrics used to distinguish Storage vs Legacy problems, which is particularly important for a mode whose purpose is to monitor divergence/failures between the two stores.

Storage.Update failure is recorded via recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration

Same issue as in Create: on the error path of Update, `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` is invoked for a failure that occurred in `d.Storage.Update`, not in Legacy. This mislabels the metric and makes it impossible to reliably distinguish storage failures from legacy failures via metrics.

Tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write actually happens

TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Delete, TestMode3_Update and TestMode3_DeleteCollection configure mock expectations on the Legacy storage (`setupLegacyFn`) but the dual writer now calls Legacy asynchronously in a goroutine launched just before Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return. The tests return immediately after asserting on the result of the synchronous Storage call, without any synchronization (no WaitGroup, channel, or sleep) and without calling `m.AssertExpectations(t)`/`AssertCalled`. As a result, these tests do not actually verify that the legacy write occurs, and would still pass even if the async legacy call were removed entirely or always failed, leaving the core 'dual write' behavior of mode 3 effectively untested.

Unrecovered panics inside the async legacy-write goroutines will crash the whole process

Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection each spawn a bare `go func() { ... }()` that calls into `d.Legacy.*` with no `recover()`. Any panic raised inside these goroutines (e.g. a nil-pointer dereference or type assertion failure in the legacy storage implementation) is not caught by the HTTP server's per-request panic-recovery middleware, because it runs on a goroutine that outlives the request handler. An unrecovered panic in a goroutine terminates the entire Go process, so a single bad legacy write could take down the whole apiserver instead of merely failing one request, which is a significant regression in robustness compared to the previous synchronous implementation.

Update no longer wraps the Legacy update with the already-resolved object, risking resourceVersion/precondition failures on every legacy write

The previous Mode3 implementation (removed by this diff) called `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, &updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}, ...)`, deliberately feeding Legacy the already-resolved object produced by Storage.Update instead of letting Legacy re-derive it. The new code instead passes the raw `objInfo` straight to `d.Legacy.Update` (line 139). Internally, Legacy.Update will fetch its own 'old' object and call `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld)`/check preconditions again, but the resourceVersion embedded in the request (and any client-supplied preconditions) reflects Storage's state, not Legacy's independently-versioned object. Since reads in mode 3 only go through Storage, Legacy's resourceVersion will generally not match, which is very likely to cause every asynchronous legacy update to fail with a conflict error, silently breaking the legacy-sync safety net for Update that this PR is supposed to provide.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check after acquiring write lock causes redundant work

After acquiring the write lock (line 48-49), the code does not re-check whether entryPointAssetsCache is already populated and the environment is non-Dev before redoing the (potentially expensive) file/CDN read. Multiple goroutines that pass the initial RLock check with ret == nil (e.g. at startup, before the cache has been populated) will each serialize on the write lock and redundantly re-read the manifest file or re-fetch from the CDN, overwriting the cache with the same result each time. This defeats much of the purpose of caching for concurrent initial requests and can add unnecessary I/O latency under load. The fix should re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` right after acquiring the write lock and return early if so.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No test added to verify the data race fix

This PR's stated purpose is fixing a data race in GetWebAssets, but no test (e.g. a concurrent-call test runnable with `go test -race`) was added to verify that the race is actually fixed or to guard against regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could silently reintroduce the race on the shared entryPointAssetsCache global.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions() contains dead/confusing logic that always returns false

The helper computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then has `if enabled { return false }` followed by an unconditional `return false`. Both branches return false, so the function always disables SQL expressions regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle state. While the intended effect (permanently disabling the vulnerable feature) matches the goal of this security PR, the code reads as though the feature flag controls the outcome when it actually has no effect at all. There is no comment explaining this is a deliberate kill-switch for CVE-2024-9264. A future maintainer could easily 'simplify' this apparent dead code (e.g. by returning `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)` directly) and unknowingly re-enable the vulnerable SQL expression code path, since nothing in the code documents why it must always be false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Misleading error message for a feature that is deliberately disabled, not unimplemented

When a SQL expression query is submitted, `ReadQuery` now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". This is inaccurate: the feature was previously implemented and working, and is being force-disabled here as an emergency security mitigation (CVE-2024-9264), not because it was never built. Users/admins who had the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle enabled before upgrading will see a confusing message that doesn't reflect the real reason the feature stopped working, making it harder to diagnose the regression after upgrade.

No tests added or updated to verify the SQL-expressions disablement, likely breaking existing coverage

This PR replaces the DuckDB-backed `DB` implementation with a stub whose `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` methods unconditionally return `errors.New("not implemented")`, and pairs it with a reader.go change that unconditionally rejects QueryTypeSQL. No test files are included in the diff, yet pkg/expr/sql/parser.go (table extraction via DuckDB AST parsing) and pkg/expr/sql_command.go (SQL command execution) are exactly the kind of logic that would normally have unit tests asserting successful parsing/execution against a real DuckDB instance. Those pre-existing tests, if they exist, would now fail since every call into the stub returns an error instead of real results, and this PR does not update or remove them. Additionally, for a PR whose explicit purpose is to close an RCE/LFI vulnerability, there is no new regression test asserting that `ReadQuery` rejects SQL expression queries regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle state, or that the stub DB always errors. Without such tests, there is no CI safety net to catch an accidental future re-enablement of the vulnerable path.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key to race

The previous code held `b.cacheMu.Lock()` for the entire `BuildIndex` function, which incidentally serialized all builds for the same NamespacedResource key (even though it hurt cross-namespace concurrency). This PR removes that lock and only takes `cacheMu` around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write (lines 137-139). However, nothing now prevents two goroutines from concurrently calling `BuildIndex` for the *same* key - this happens in practice via `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` (resource/search.go), which is called on every `Search` RPC and on every watch event, and performs an unlocked `GetIndex` read followed by a `build` call on cache miss. If two concurrent requests for a newly-seen (or not-yet-indexed, e.g. small/skipped-at-startup) namespace both see a nil index, they will both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` against the same on-disk directory concurrently (line 98), which can fail or corrupt the index, and will both finish and overwrite `b.cache[key]`, wasting work and potentially leaving an index object whose underlying bleve.Index was already closed/overwritten. This is a regression introduced by the finer-grained locking change, not just a perf improvement.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
No test added for the new fine-grained locking behavior in BuildIndex

The change to `BuildIndex` narrows the locked section from the whole function to just the final cache-map write, explicitly to improve concurrency when building indexes for many namespaces at once. This is a concurrency-sensitive change (see related finding about same-key concurrent builds), yet no test was added to exercise concurrent `BuildIndex`/`GetOrCreateIndex` calls (e.g. with `-race`) to confirm the new locking scheme is safe for repeated/parallel calls for the same key, or that cross-key builds genuinely run in parallel as intended.

Postgres integration test silently skipped with no tracking issue

The test now unconditionally skips when `GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres` with the comment 'skipping - test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' This removes postgres coverage for `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` from CI without a linked tracking issue or explanation of what is failing, making it easy for this gap to be forgotten and for a real postgres-specific regression to go undetected going forward.

Removing per-RPC Init() guards removes the only safety net if initialization wasn't performed

Every RPC method (`Create`, `Update`, `Delete`, `Read`, `List`, `Watch`, `Search`, `History`, `Origin`, `IsHealthy`, `PutBlob`, `GetBlob`) previously called `s.Init(ctx)` defensively before doing any work, which both lazily initialized the server and acted as a guard against using an uninitialized `server` (e.g. `s.broadcaster` being nil, which would be used at `s.broadcaster.Subscribe(ctx)` in `Watch`). These guards are all removed on the assumption that `NewResourceServer` always performs `Init` before returning the server. Any code path that constructs a `server` value without going through `NewResourceServer` (e.g. test helpers within the `resource` package) will now hit a nil-pointer dereference on `s.broadcaster` (or other uninitialized fields) in `Watch`, rather than the previous lazy fallback. The PR description itself raises this exact risk ('Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?') and it isn't verified or addressed in the diff.

Resource server construction now blocks indefinitely on full search index build with no timeout

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously before returning the constructed server. `Init` calls `s.search.init(ctx)`, which performs a full index build across every namespace returned by `GetResourceStats` using a background context with no deadline. For installations with many/large namespaces this can take a long time (this is literally called out in the PR description as the reason gRPC calls were timing out). Moving this work into the constructor removes the context-cancellation symptom but replaces it with an unbounded blocking call during process/module startup, which can now cause the whole module server (not just a single RPC) to hang past readiness/liveness probe timeouts or deployment rollout windows, with no partial availability and no circuit breaker. This tradeoff (named explicitly as an open question by the PR author: 'What could this break?') should be called out/resolved before merging, e.g. by bounding the startup init with a timeout or making it async with a readiness gate.

Shared `err` and counter variables mutated unsynchronized across the errgroup goroutines in searchSupport.init

In `searchSupport.init`, `err` (declared from `stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed` are captured by every goroutine launched in `group.Go(...)` (lines 186-193) and written concurrently without any synchronization (`totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`), then `err` is read back and returned from each goroutine, and `totalBatchesIndexed` is read after `group.Wait()` for a trace attribute. This is a data race: one goroutine's error result can be clobbered by another before it reads it back to return to the errgroup, meaning `group.Wait()`/`s.initErr` can reflect the wrong build's error (masking a real failure or spuriously failing because of an unrelated goroutine's transient error), and `totalBatchesIndexed` can under-count due to lost updates. Because `NewResourceServer` now calls this `init` synchronously at startup (previously it only ran lazily on the first gRPC call), this race is exercised on every process startup instead of occasionally, increasing the chance that a single namespace's indexing error incorrectly fails (or incorrectly succeeds) server construction for all tenants.

Trace context propagation fix applied inconsistently - only one of several call sites updated

The PR fixes `GetResourceStats` (line 126) to reassign `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` so the derived span context is propagated into the subsequent `b.db.WithTx(ctx, ...)` call, matching the PR's stated goal of 'fixing trace propagation by passing span contexts down'. However, the same pattern (`_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` discarding the new ctx) remains unfixed in other methods in this same file, e.g. `WriteEvent` (line 158), `ReadResource` (line 353), and `ListIterator` (line 388). In each of these, child operations (`dbutil.Exec`, `dbutil.QueryRow`, `dbutil.QueryRows`, nested `WithTx` calls) continue to use the original, non-span context, so trace propagation remains broken for most of the SQL backend despite the PR claiming to address it. This is misleading for anyone reviewing the trace-fix claim and leaves most of the intended fix undone.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup references the literal alias "alias" instead of the actual created IDP alias, leaking test data

In the new testCacheIDPForLogin test, cleanup is registered with `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` (also repeated at line 425 for the "idp-alias-20" provider). The literal string "alias" is passed instead of the actual alias used when creating the provider (e.g. "idp-alias-" + i). This means the cleanup never removes the 20+ identity providers created by the test; at best the cleanup call fails (no IDP with alias "alias" exists), and the created identity providers remain in the realm after the test finishes. This leftover state can pollute subsequent tests in the same realm (e.g. IDP count assertions, alias uniqueness on re-run, or other cache tests), causing flaky or order-dependent test failures.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
No test coverage for invalidating warm login caches via create()/remove() of a currently login-eligible IDP

testCacheIDPForLogin only exercises the create()/remove() invalidation paths (registerIDPLoginInvalidation) with IDPs that do NOT qualify for login (e.g. `testRealm().identityProviders().get("idp-alias-1").remove()` removes a disabled, non-login IDP, and the newly created idp-alias-20 is initially hideOnLogin=true). The 20 initial IDP creations happen before any cache is warmed, so they never actually exercise invalidation of a populated cache either. As a result, the scenario where a currently login-eligible IDP is created or removed after the login caches are already populated (which should trigger registerIDPLoginInvalidation to clear all FetchMode caches) is never verified; only the analogous update() path (registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate) is thoroughly tested. A regression in the create()/remove() invalidation logic for this case would not be caught by this test.

remove() now unconditionally hits the underlying JPA store even when the IDP is already cached

In remove(), `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is now executed unconditionally before the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` check. Previously, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` was only called inside the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` branch; when the cache entry was valid, the code used the already-cached `CachedIdentityProvider` (`cached.getIdentityProvider()`) without touching the delegate at all. After this change, every call to remove() performs an extra round-trip to the underlying storage (JPA/DB) even in the common case where the alias is already present in cache, which is pure overhead introduced only to support the new `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` call. The same information could be derived from `cached.getIdentityProvider()` in the else-branch instead of re-fetching from the delegate, avoiding the redundant query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return a BouncyCastle provider

`CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` is documented (in the interface) as returning "BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider". This implementation instead returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a typical JVM resolves to the JDK's built-in keystore provider (e.g. SUN), not BouncyCastle at all. Unlike every other unimplemented method in this class, which consistently throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, this method silently returns a semantically wrong value, which can mislead any caller that relies on the contract (e.g. comparing/using the provider for BC-specific operations). It should either throw `UnsupportedOperationException` like the rest of the unimplemented methods, or be documented/implemented correctly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Inside `concatenatedRSToASN1DER`, the two lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create throwaway ASN1Encoder instances, encode the BigIntegers into them, and then discard the result without ever using it - the method immediately re-creates new encoders a few lines below to build the actual return value. This is leftover/dead code that wastes CPU cycles on every signature conversion and signals the implementation wasn't cleaned up before merging; it should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks source compatibility for existing CryptoProvider implementations

`CryptoProvider` is a public interface loaded via ServiceLoader/SPI and is implemented both inside and (potentially) outside this repository. Adding `int order();` as a new abstract method (no default implementation) means any existing implementation of this interface that is not updated in lock-step will fail to compile/break until it adds an `order()` override. Since this is a published API in the `common` module, this is a source-compatibility break for downstream custom CryptoProvider implementations. A default method (e.g. returning a baseline value) would avoid breaking existing implementors while still allowing providers that need preference to override it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple CryptoProviders on classpath are now silently resolved instead of failing fast, with only debug-level logging

Previously, `detectProvider` threw an `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found on the classpath, forcing an explicit fix of classpath/packaging issues. The new code silently picks the provider with the highest `order()` and only logs the ignored providers via `logger.debugf(...)`, which is typically disabled in production. This means a classpath misconfiguration that places two different CryptoProvider implementations on the classpath (e.g. accidentally bundling both FIPS and non-FIPS crypto modules) will no longer fail at startup and will instead silently run with whichever provider happens to have the higher `order()` value, without any visible warning in default logs. This can hide serious security/operational misconfigurations (e.g., running non-FIPS crypto when FIPS mode was intended) that used to be caught immediately.

No test coverage for the new multi-provider ordering/selection logic

`detectProvider` now sorts discovered `CryptoProvider` instances by `order()` (descending) and picks the first one instead of throwing when multiple are present. This is a meaningful behavioral change (see related finding about silent provider selection), but no unit test was added to verify that, given multiple CryptoProviders with different `order()` values on the classpath, the correct (highest-order) one is selected and the others are merely logged rather than causing failure.

Single EC key pair of a default curve reused across ES256/ES384/ES512 tests

The constructor generates a single `KeyPair` via `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` without specifying a curve, which will typically produce a P-256 (secp256r1) key pair. This same key pair is then reused for `testES256`, `testES384`, and `testES512`. Signing with SHA-384/SHA-512 using a P-256 key does not produce signatures whose R/S components match the natural lengths expected for ES384/ES512 (which are meant to be used with P-384/P-521 keys respectively). As a result, the tests don't exercise the ASN.1 encode/decode logic with realistically-sized R/S integers for the larger curves (e.g., the extra sign-byte handling that occurs with 66-byte P-521 integers), reducing the value of the ES384/ES512 test cases and potentially masking edge-case bugs that would only manifest with correctly-sized keys.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission cannot return real client IDs and can return the bogus literal 'Clients'

getClientsWithPermission() iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) and adds resource.getName() to the result for any matching resource with the given scope granted. However, per-client resources created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() (server-spi-private .../AdminPermissionsSchema.java, around line 104) are never given a 'type' attribute (only resource.updateScopes(...) is called, there is no resource.setType(resourceType)), so findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) will never match them - individual per-client granted permissions are silently excluded from the result. Conversely, the catch-all 'all clients' resource created in AdminPermissionsSchema.init() does have its type explicitly set to CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE and its name is literally the string 'Clients'. If an all-clients permission for the requested scope exists, that resource matches findByType and the literal string 'Clients' gets added to the returned Set<String> as if it were an actual client ID. Any caller treating the result as a set of real client identifiers will get incorrect/garbage data.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NullPointerException when the 'all-clients' resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), if the per-client resource is not found, the code falls back to resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE), and then immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking whether getResourceTypeResource returned null. If the 'Clients' catch-all resource does not exist for the resource server (e.g. schema not initialized for that resource server, or data inconsistency), resource will be null and findByResource(server, null) is likely to throw an NPE (and if it somehow doesn't, resource.getScopes() later in the method would).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client/role/group removal cleanup can crash with UnsupportedOperationException when V2 evaluator is selected

The ProviderEventListener registered here calls management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false) (and similarly for roles/groups) when a RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent occurs. The whole block is now gated by Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) (line 77), but the inner call to management() independently decides between V1 and V2 based on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. If both the legacy ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ and the new ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 feature flags are enabled at the same time (nothing in this code prevents that, and both are server-wide flags), management() will return MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients().setPermissionsEnabled() (and similarly users()/groups() for the respective events) now throws UnsupportedOperationException unconditionally (see ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled). This exception would propagate out of the event listener during a client/role/group deletion, breaking that admin operation.

Missing test coverage for Clients resource-type permission CRUD/resource lifecycle and getClientsWithPermission

UserResourceTypePermissionTest provides dedicated coverage for permission/resource representation semantics for the Users resource type (testCreateResourceTypePermission, testCreateResourceObjectPermission, testFindByResourceObject, testDelete - verifying orphan resource cleanup, and testUpdate). PermissionClientTest, added by this PR for the new Clients resource type, only contains behavioral tests (manage/configure/view/mapRoles scenarios) and has no equivalent tests verifying that creating/removing scope permissions for Clients correctly creates/cleans up the underlying Resource records, nor any test exercising ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission(). Given the identified bug in getClientsWithPermission (not finding real per-client resources, and potentially returning the literal 'Clients'), this gap means the regression would not be caught by the test suite.

canExchangeTo/exchangeToPermission now unconditionally throw UnsupportedOperationException, breaking standard OAuth2 token exchange

ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo() (and exchangeToPermission()) unconditionally throw UnsupportedOperationException. Before this PR, MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() was not overridden, so calls to AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(...) fell back to the legacy, functional ClientPermissions implementation even when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 was enabled. Now that MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, any call to canExchangeTo (used by the standard OAuth2 token-exchange grant to check the per-client 'token-exchange' permission) will throw an unchecked RuntimeException instead of evaluating/denying the request. Because AdminPermissions.management(...) dispatches to V2 purely based on the global Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 flag (not a per-realm setting), enabling this preview feature on a server breaks token exchange for every client in every realm on that server, not just realms that opted into the new permission schema.

getResourceName() was not updated to handle the new CLIENTS resource type

getResourceName() special-cases USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE (returning 'All users' for the catch-all resource and the username for individual user resources) but has no corresponding branch for CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE even though this PR adds Clients as a fully supported resource type. For permissions targeting Clients, this method falls through to 'return resource.getDisplayName();', which, for resources created via getOrCreateResource/resourceStore.create (no display name set), returns the raw resource name - the client's internal UUID rather than a friendly label like 'All clients' or the client's clientId. This produces a poor/incorrect UX anywhere this name is surfaced (e.g. admin console or REST responses listing permissions for the Clients resource type).

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silent reassignment of RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 changes the exit-code contract for existing users

This change moves `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` from 4 to 3 and reuses 4 for the new `FEATURE_DISABLED` code. Prior to this PR, any scripts/automation built against the previously-released preview `update-compatibility check` command that interpreted exit code 4 as 'recreate upgrade required' will now observe exit code 4 meaning 'feature disabled' and exit code 3 meaning 'recreate required' — a behavior change with no migration note, deprecation warning, or changelog entry in the diff. Even though the tool is labeled preview, this is a backward-incompatible change to a documented, script-facing contract (the exit codes are explicitly called out in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc as being safe to depend on), and should be called out explicitly (e.g., in release notes) so existing preview adopters are not silently broken.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION note overstates when the rolling-updates feature flag is required

The newly added CAUTION block states unconditionally: 'While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' This is placed directly under the 'Managing Keycloak Operator Updates' heading, before any explanation of the default behavior. However, the immediately following NOTE says that when `update.strategy` is left unset, the Operator defaults to mimicking the pre-existing (26.1 and older) behavior with no mention of needing the feature flag. This is corroborated by operator/src/test/java/.../UpgradeTest.java, where `createInitialDeployment` only enables the `rolling-updates` feature when an explicit `UpdateStrategy` (e.g. RECREATE) is configured, and returns early (without enabling the feature) when `updateStrategy == null`. So the feature flag is only required when explicitly setting `update.strategy`, not for using the Operator's update mechanism in general. As written, the CAUTION note will mislead readers into thinking they must always enable `rolling-updates` or the Operator will fail, even when relying on default behavior.

Feature-disabled gating is only tested for the metadata subcommand, and exit code is never asserted

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only launches `UpdateCompatibility.NAME, UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.NAME` without the feature flag and checks the error message. The identical feature-gating logic was also added to `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` (quarkus/runtime/.../UpdateCompatibilityCheck.java), but there is no test exercising the `check` subcommand with the feature disabled. Additionally, the test never asserts the actual exit code (`CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED` = 4), even though the documentation (docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc) explicitly documents exit code 4 as the contract for 'feature disabled', and this exit code is meant to be relied upon by automation. Without an assertion on the exit code and without coverage of the `check` subcommand, a regression in either path (e.g., wrong exit code, or the check subcommand silently allowing use when the feature is disabled) would not be caught by tests.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group-wide canManage() grants manage rights to callers that only have VIEW permission

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (the no-arg, "all groups" variant), the permission check is `hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)` – i.e. it treats VIEW as sufficient to satisfy a manage check. Compare this with the per-group override `canManage(GroupModel group)` a few lines below, which correctly checks only `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE`. Because `requireManage()` (used e.g. by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() to guard creating top-level groups) ultimately calls this no-arg canManage(), any admin who was only granted the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource is incorrectly treated as having manage rights and can create/modify groups. This is a privilege-escalation bug; it should check AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE only, matching canManage(GroupModel).

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() passes the Resource's internal id instead of the group id, breaking the lookup and the returned ids

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), the lambda receives `groupResource` (a Resource found via findByType) and calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)` and `granted.add(groupResource.getId())`. Everywhere else in this class (canView(GroupModel), canManage(GroupModel), canViewMembers, canManageMembers, canManageMembership) the lookup key passed to hasPermission is `group.getId()` – the actual GroupModel id, which is also the value AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() uses as the Resource's *name* when the resource is created. Resource.getId() is a separate, internally-generated identifier that does not equal the resource's name. As a result, the internal `hasPermission(groupId, ...)` call does `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` with the wrong value, which will not find the correct resource and will instead always fall back to the catch-all "Groups" resource-type resource. In addition, the ids placed into the returned `granted` set are resource ids, not actual group ids, so callers (UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource) that use this set to filter by `UserModel.GROUPS` will never match real group memberships. This breaks per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS based user visibility for V2 admin permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing negative test that VIEW-only all-groups permission does not grant manage capability

testManageAllGroups() only verifies that granting MANAGE on the all-groups resource allows creating/updating groups; there is no test asserting that an admin granted only VIEW on the all-groups resource is still forbidden from creating/updating/deleting groups. Such a test would have caught the bug in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() where hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) incorrectly allows VIEW to satisfy a manage check.

Undocumented behavior change: canViewMembers(group) now also honors MANAGE_MEMBERS scope

In GroupPermissions.canViewMembers(GroupModel), the scope check was widened from `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE)` to `hasPermission(group, VIEW_MEMBERS_SCOPE, MANAGE_MEMBERS_SCOPE)`. This is part of the stable (GA) ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature, not the new V2 feature this PR is adding. The PR description only mentions adding Groups resource type/scopes to the V2 authorization schema, so this silent semantic change to the existing V1 group-members view permission is undocumented and untested for V1 (the new tests target only the V2/KeycloakAdminPermissionsServerConfig path). Existing V1 deployments relying on manage-members not implying view-members will see a behavior change.

getOrCreateResource() never tags per-resource instances with their resource type

getOrCreateResource() creates per-instance resources (for Users, Clients, and now Groups) via `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` but never calls `resource.setType(resourceType)` on them, unlike the "all-resource" resources created in init() (which do call resource.setType(type)). Because of this, `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` used by the new GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() will not find individual per-group resources created through this method, since they were never tagged with the "Groups" type. This silently undermines any type-based resource queries introduced for the new Groups feature.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian translation replaced with Italian text

The key `totpStep1` was changed from the (stale, link-containing) Lithuanian text to `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian, not Lithuanian. This is a user-visible content defect: Lithuanian users configuring an authenticator will now see an unrelated Italian sentence instead of a Lithuanian translation. This appears to be a copy/paste mistake made while fixing the illegal anchor tags flagged by the new sanitizer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Simplified Chinese (zh_CN) file now uses Traditional Chinese phrasing

The key `totpStep1` was changed to `在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：`, which uses Traditional Chinese characters/terminology (手機, 裝, 應用程式) rather than Simplified Chinese (which would use 手机, 装, 应用). Since this file is the zh_CN (Simplified Chinese) locale resource, this introduces a script/locale inconsistency that should instead read with Simplified characters, e.g. 在您的手机上安装以下应用程序之一：

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

false_positives.candidate:
Anchor-tag validation assumes identical ordering between translation and English source

`santizeAnchors` walks through anchor tags in the translated value and the English value in lockstep using two independent `Matcher.find()` calls, requiring the Nth anchor tag in the translation to exactly equal the Nth anchor tag in English. Legitimate translations frequently reorder embedded markup (e.g. due to different sentence/grammar structure, as is common for RTL or SOV languages), which would cause a correct translation with the same set of anchors (just reordered) to be reported as "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string", a false positive that would block otherwise-valid translations from passing verification.

Choice-format normalization is hardcoded to specific key names, which will miss future keys using the same syntax

`normalizeValue` only strips MessageFormat ChoiceFormat syntax (which legitimately contains `<`) for keys matching `templateHelp`, `optimizeLookupHelp`, keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit`, or exactly `error-invalid-multivalued-size`. Any new or existing message key elsewhere in the codebase that uses `{n,choice,...}` syntax with a `<` character (a common pattern for pluralization) but isn't in this hardcoded list will be incorrectly flagged as illegal HTML by this verifier, producing false positives that block legitimate translations/content unless the hardcoded list is remembered and updated every time such a key is added.

Fragile string-substitution derivation of the English source file path

The path to the English counterpart file is computed with `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. false_positives.candidate:
error-invalid-multivalued-size rewritten with incompatible Java MessageFormat syntax, breaking i18next interpolation

The key was changed from `Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. This file is consumed by the Account Console React app via i18next, which uses double-curly-brace interpolation (`{{0}}`), as confirmed by every other key in the same file (e.g. `backTo=Back to {{app}}`, `setUpNew=Set up {{name}}`). Switching to single braces means `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` will no longer be substituted by i18next, and the Java `MessageFormat` ChoiceFormat fragment `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` is not valid i18next syntax at all, so it will be rendered verbatim to end users instead of the pluralized word. This is a functional regression in the Account Console error message, seemingly caused by blindly applying the Java-properties fix for this key to the JS i18next resource file as well.

error-invalid-multivalued-size rewritten with incompatible Java MessageFormat syntax in Admin Console i18next resources

Same issue as in the account-ui file: `error-invalid-multivalued-size=Attribute {{0}} must have at least {{1}} and at most {{2}} value(s).` was changed to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. The surrounding keys in this file use i18next double-brace interpolation, so this change breaks placeholder substitution and introduces a literal, unparsed ChoiceFormat string that will be shown to admins instead of a correctly pluralized message when editing multivalued user/client attributes.

Lithuanian login translation replaced with Italian text

The key `loginTotpStep1` was changed from the Lithuanian text (which previously contained mismatched FreeOTP/Google Play anchor tags) to `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian rather than Lithuanian. This is the same mistake as in the account messages file for the same locale and key, and results in Lithuanian users seeing Italian text on the login TOTP setup page.

Property files are read with default ISO-8859-1 decoding although they contain raw UTF-8 text

`bundle = new PropertyResourceBundle(fis)` (and the equivalent call for the English counterpart) uses the InputStream-based constructor, which per the Properties/PropertyResourceBundle contract decodes content as ISO-8859-1. The actual theme message files (as shown throughout this PR, e.g. Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic, Greek text) are UTF-8 encoded with literal multi-byte characters, not `\uXXXX`-escaped ASCII. Reading them through the InputStream constructor will corrupt all non-ASCII text used for comparisons and for the diff snippets emitted in error messages, making the tool's diagnostic output unreliable/garbled for the vast majority of real locale files. The code should decode explicitly as UTF-8 (e.g. via `InputStreamReader`/`PropertyResourceBundle(Reader)`).

Fragile string-substitution derivation of the English source file path

The path to the English counterpart file is computed with `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")`. This blindly rewrites any occurrence of the literal substring "resources-community" anywhere in the absolute path, and assumes the file name's final underscore-delimited segment is exactly the locale suffix. This is fragile: a checkout path containing "resources-community" elsewhere would be mis-rewritten, and file names containing an underscore before the locale code in a different position (e.g. a base name with an embedded underscore) will compute a non-existent English file name. In fact, the accompanying test had to rename `duplicate_keys.properties` to `duplicateKeys_en.properties` specifically to avoid the mid-name underscore being matched by this regex and resolving to a nonexistent `duplicate_en.properties`, which demonstrates the fragility of this approach in production use.

Unchecked RuntimeException thrown instead of using the MojoExecutionException error-reporting path

`verifySafeHtml()` wraps IOExceptions (e.g. missing/English file not found) in `RuntimeException` rather than propagating through the `MojoExecutionException` used by `verify()`/`verifyNoDuplicateKeys`. Since `verify()`'s try/catch only catches `IOException`, any IO failure inside `verifySafeHtml()` surfaces as an unchecked `RuntimeException` with a raw stack trace rather than being reported through the structured `messages` list or wrapped the same way other failures are, producing an inconsistent and less actionable failure mode for the Maven build.

Choice-format normalization is hardcoded to specific key names, which will miss future keys using the same syntax

`normalizeValue` only strips MessageFormat ChoiceFormat syntax (which legitimately contains `<`) for keys matching `templateHelp`, `optimizeLookupHelp`, keys starting with `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit`, or exactly `error-invalid-multivalued-size`. Any new or existing message key elsewhere in the codebase that uses `{n,choice,...}` syntax with a `<` character (a common pattern for pluralization) but isn't in this hardcoded list will be incorrectly flagged as illegal HTML by this verifier, producing false positives that block legitimate translations/content unless the hardcoded list is remembered and updated every time such a key is added.

Anchor-tag validation assumes identical ordering between translation and English source

`santizeAnchors` walks through anchor tags in the translated value and the English value in lockstep using two independent `Matcher.find()` calls, requiring the Nth anchor tag in the translation to exactly equal the Nth anchor tag in English. Legitimate translations frequently reorder embedded markup (e.g. due to different sentence/grammar structure, as is common for RTL or SOV languages), which would cause a correct translation with the same set of anchors (just reordered) to be reported as "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string", a false positive that would block otherwise-valid translations from passing verification.

No test coverage for non-ASCII/UTF-8 property content

All added test fixtures (`illegalHtmlTag_en.properties`, `noHtml_en.properties`, `noHtml_de.properties`, `changedAnchor_en.properties`, `changedAnchor_de.properties`) use plain ASCII content. None of the tests exercise a file containing multi-byte UTF-8 characters (Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic, etc.), even though essentially all real translated message files in this repository contain such content and the tool reads files via an InputStream-based `PropertyResourceBundle` that decodes as ISO-8859-1. This gap means the encoding-corruption problem for non-ASCII translations is not caught by the test suite.

Copy-paste bug: rawTokenId null-check is never performed

In the AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull call uses the `grantType` variable again instead of `rawTokenId`:
```
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null grantType not allowed");
Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");
```
As written, `rawTokenId` is never validated for null. If a caller passes a null rawTokenId (e.g. a bug in a custom TokenContextEncoderProvider, or future refactors), the AccessTokenContext will silently store a null rawTokenId, which will later be concatenated in `encodeTokenId()` producing a token id ending in the literal string "null" instead of failing fast with a clear error message.
