true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId() grant-shortcut check is logically inverted and off-by-one, so it never actually validates the grant type

The new helper `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)` is supposed to verify that the encoded access-token id contains the expected grant-type shortcut (at positions 4-5 of the 6-character context prefix, per DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider's encoding: sessionType[0-1] + tokenType[2-3] + grantType[4-5]). The implementation has two combined defects:
1. It extracts `items[0].substring(3, 5)` instead of `substring(4, 6)`, so it reads the wrong characters (half of the tokenType shortcut and half of the grantType shortcut) rather than the actual grant-type shortcut.
2. The condition is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns a non-match precisely when the (wrongly extracted) substring equals the expected value, instead of returning a non-match when it does NOT equal the expected value.
Because of the wrong substring range, the extracted characters will essentially never equal `expectedGrantShortcut`, so the `if` branch is effectively never taken and the method degenerates into validating only that the raw id part is a UUID. This means all the call sites that were updated to use this helper (expectCodeToToken, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectAuthReqIdToToken) do not actually assert that the correct grant-type shortcut was embedded in the token id, silently defeating the purpose of the new assertion and hiding future regressions in the grant-type encoding.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies both defects described by the golden comment: the grant shortcut must be extracted with substring(4,6), and a matching shortcut should contribute to a true result alongside UUID validation rather than return false.

false_positives.candidate:
New mandatory getShortcut() method breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

A new abstract method `String getShortcut();` was added to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory provider-factory interface with no default implementation. Any existing third-party/custom implementation of this SPI (grant types are a documented extension point) will fail to compile/deploy until it implements this new method, and any already-compiled custom provider will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when loaded against the new interface. This is a breaking SPI change that should at least be called out as such (or given a default implementation) given it is not accompanied by any deprecation path.

Backward-incompatible change to access-token id (jti) format is not documented

`initToken()` now prefixes every access-token id with a 6-character encoded context (session type + token type + grant type) before the previously plain UUID, e.g. `onrtac:1f65761e-...` instead of a bare UUID. This changes the format of the `jti` claim for every access token issued by Keycloak going forward. Any external system, log parser, SIEM rule, or client integration that validates/parses the token id as a plain UUID (36 chars, specific dash positions) will break. The PR does not include any upgrade-guide note, migration documentation, or changelog entry describing this change in token id format, even though it affects every issued access token by default with no opt-out configuration (only an SPI override is possible, which requires writing custom provider code).

Duplicate-shortcut validation logic in postInit() has no test coverage

postInit() contains important validation logic that throws an IllegalStateException if two registered OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations collide on id or shortcut (`grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()`). This is the only safety net preventing silently incorrect token-id decoding when a new grant type is added with a clashing shortcut. The added DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest only exercises DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider with hand-built maps and never calls postInit() with a real (or fake) KeycloakSessionFactory/provider-factory stream, so this validation path is completely untested.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery-code metadata (hash, label, timestamp) is dropped when delegating to a UserStorageProvider

createRecoveryCodesCredential() builds a plain UserCredentialModel containing only the raw, unhashed JSON list of generated codes (recoveryCodesJson) and passes that to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). The already-built RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel passed into the method (which contains the hashed codes, the user-chosen label and the generation timestamp) is only used on the local-storage fallback path and is discarded whenever a UserStorageProvider accepts the update. Any UserStorageProvider implementation therefore receives raw codes and no label/timestamp, and must re-implement hashing and reconstruct metadata itself (or lose it entirely, as the shipped reference implementation does). This is a real loss of functionality/metadata for the new 'recovery codes in user storage' feature, not just a theoretical concern, since the included test provider demonstrates exactly this loss.

Recovery codes are persisted unhashed in the reference UserStorageProvider implementation

In updateCredential(), the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE branch stores input.getChallengeResponse() (the raw, unhashed JSON array of generated recovery codes) directly as credentialData with no hashing, unlike how the local DB-backed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider stores codes (hashed). This is the provider shipped as the reference/test implementation for the new 'store recovery codes in user storage' feature, and it stores backup authentication codes in cleartext, which is an insecure pattern that could be copied by real implementers of UserStorageProvider.

Recovery codes validated through the user-storage provider are never marked as consumed, allowing infinite reuse

isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))` and never removes/marks the matched code as used, nor persists any updated state back to `myUser.recoveryCodes`. Recovery/backup codes are meant to be single-use; with this implementation the exact same code can be used to authenticate an unlimited number of times when the credential is stored via this UserStorageProvider, defeating the core security property of recovery codes. Because the integration test (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) only logs in once, this defect is not caught by the new tests.

getCredentials() can throw NullPointerException when the user is unknown to this storage

getCredentials(RealmModel, UserModel) calls `getMyUser(user)` and then immediately dereferences `myUser.recoveryCodes`/`myUser.otp` without checking `myUser != null`. Every other method in this class that uses getMyUser() (getDisableableCredentialTypesStream, isConfiguredFor) explicitly guards against a null result, but this new method does not, so a call for a user not present in the backing map will throw an NPE instead of returning an empty stream.

New recovery-codes-in-user-storage test does not cover code consumption, reuse prevention, or credential removal

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin only sets up recovery codes in the custom user storage and performs a single successful login with one code. It never verifies that a used code cannot be reused, that the credential is removed/required action re-added once all codes are consumed (mirroring RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator's allCodesUsed()/removeStoredCredentialById logic), or that disabling/removing the credential works for the federated case (as is done for OTP in testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin and testDisableCredentialsInUserStorage). As a result, the actual data-integrity bug in the shipped BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid() (codes never consumed) goes undetected.

Hard-coded credential provider id instead of the existing constant

createRecoveryCodesCredential() looks up the provider with the literal string "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes" instead of RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory.PROVIDER_ID, which was previously referenced directly (and imported) in RecoveryAuthnCodesAction before this change removed that import. Using a magic string loses compile-time safety: if the provider id ever changes, this call will silently fail at runtime (NPE from session.getProvider returning null) instead of failing to compile.

New getCredentials() override also changes existing OTP credential exposure, outside the scope of the recovery-codes feature

To support the new feature, updateCredential() now assigns a real generated id to the OTP CredentialModel (newOTP.setId(KeycloakModelUtils.generateId())), and the newly added getCredentials() override unconditionally includes myUser.getOtp() whenever an OTP credential exists. Previously this provider did not implement getCredentials(), so OTP credentials were not exposed through the generic federated-credential discovery path at all. This is a behavior change for OTP handling in this provider that is incidental to the recovery-codes feature and is not covered by any new or existing test specifically validating that OTP account-management flows (e.g. listing/deleting OTP credentials via account REST) still behave the same with this newly real, generated credential id.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silent reassignment of RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 changes the exit-code contract for existing users

This change moves `RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` from 4 to 3 and reuses 4 for the new `FEATURE_DISABLED` code. Prior to this PR, any scripts/automation built against the previously-released preview `update-compatibility check` command that interpreted exit code 4 as 'recreate upgrade required' will now observe exit code 4 meaning 'feature disabled' and exit code 3 meaning 'recreate required' — a behavior change with no migration note, deprecation warning, or changelog entry in the diff. Even though the tool is labeled preview, this is a backward-incompatible change to a documented, script-facing contract (the exit codes are explicitly called out in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc as being safe to depend on), and should be called out explicitly (e.g., in release notes) so existing preview adopters are not silently broken.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing changelog/release documentation and migration guidance for the exit-code change, explaining its impact on existing scripts and explicitly requesting release notes.

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION note overstates when the rolling-updates feature flag is required

The newly added CAUTION block states unconditionally: 'While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' This is placed directly under the 'Managing Keycloak Operator Updates' heading, before any explanation of the default behavior. However, the immediately following NOTE says that when `update.strategy` is left unset, the Operator defaults to mimicking the pre-existing (26.1 and older) behavior with no mention of needing the feature flag. This is corroborated by operator/src/test/java/.../UpgradeTest.java, where `createInitialDeployment` only enables the `rolling-updates` feature when an explicit `UpdateStrategy` (e.g. RECREATE) is configured, and returns early (without enabling the feature) when `updateStrategy == null`. So the feature flag is only required when explicitly setting `update.strategy`, not for using the Operator's update mechanism in general. As written, the CAUTION note will mislead readers into thinking they must always enable `rolling-updates` or the Operator will fail, even when relying on default behavior.

Feature-disabled gating is only tested for the metadata subcommand, and exit code is never asserted

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only launches `UpdateCompatibility.NAME, UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.NAME` without the feature flag and checks the error message. The identical feature-gating logic was also added to `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` (quarkus/runtime/.../UpdateCompatibilityCheck.java), but there is no test exercising the `check` subcommand with the feature disabled. Additionally, the test never asserts the actual exit code (`CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED` = 4), even though the documentation (docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc) explicitly documents exit code 4 as the contract for 'feature disabled', and this exit code is meant to be relied upon by automation. Without an assertion on the exit code and without coverage of the `check` subcommand, a regression in either path (e.g., wrong exit code, or the check subcommand silently allowing use when the feature is disabled) would not be caught by tests.

getClientsWithPermission() iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) and adds resource.getName() to the result for any matching resource with the given scope granted. However, per-client resources created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() (server-spi-private .../AdminPermissionsSchema.java, around line 104) are never given a 'type' attribute (only resource.updateScopes(...) is called, there is no resource.setType(resourceType)), so findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) will never match them - individual per-client granted permissions are silently excluded from the result. true_positives.matched_candidate:

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), if the per-client resource is not found, the code falls back to resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE), and then immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking whether getResourceTypeResource returned null. false_positives.candidate:
canExchangeTo/exchangeToPermission now unconditionally throw UnsupportedOperationException, breaking standard OAuth2 token exchange

ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo() (and exchangeToPermission()) unconditionally throw UnsupportedOperationException. Before this PR, MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() was not overridden, so calls to AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(...) fell back to the legacy, functional ClientPermissions implementation even when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 was enabled. Now that MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, any call to canExchangeTo (used by the standard OAuth2 token-exchange grant to check the per-client 'token-exchange' permission) will throw an unchecked RuntimeException instead of evaluating/denying the request. Because AdminPermissions.management(...) dispatches to V2 purely based on the global Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 flag (not a per-realm setting), enabling this preview feature on a server breaks token exchange for every client in every realm on that server, not just realms that opted into the new permission schema.

Client/role/group removal cleanup can crash with UnsupportedOperationException when V2 evaluator is selected

The ProviderEventListener registered here calls management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false) (and similarly for roles/groups) when a RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent occurs. The whole block is now gated by Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) (line 77), but the inner call to management() independently decides between V1 and V2 based on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. If both the legacy ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ and the new ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 feature flags are enabled at the same time (nothing in this code prevents that, and both are server-wide flags), management() will return MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients().setPermissionsEnabled() (and similarly users()/groups() for the respective events) now throws UnsupportedOperationException unconditionally (see ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled). This exception would propagate out of the event listener during a client/role/group deletion, breaking that admin operation.

getResourceName() was not updated to handle the new CLIENTS resource type

getResourceName() special-cases USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE (returning 'All users' for the catch-all resource and the username for individual user resources) but has no corresponding branch for CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE even though this PR adds Clients as a fully supported resource type. For permissions targeting Clients, this method falls through to 'return resource.getDisplayName();', which, for resources created via getOrCreateResource/resourceStore.create (no display name set), returns the raw resource name - the client's internal UUID rather than a friendly label like 'All clients' or the client's clientId. This produces a poor/incorrect UX anywhere this name is surfaced (e.g. admin console or REST responses listing permissions for the Clients resource type).

Missing test coverage for Clients resource-type permission CRUD/resource lifecycle and getClientsWithPermission

UserResourceTypePermissionTest provides dedicated coverage for permission/resource representation semantics for the Users resource type (testCreateResourceTypePermission, testCreateResourceObjectPermission, testFindByResourceObject, testDelete - verifying orphan resource cleanup, and testUpdate). PermissionClientTest, added by this PR for the new Clients resource type, only contains behavioral tests (manage/configure/view/mapRoles scenarios) and has no equivalent tests verifying that creating/removing scope permissions for Clients correctly creates/cleans up the underlying Resource records, nor any test exercising ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission(). Given the identified bug in getClientsWithPermission (not finding real per-client resources, and potentially returning the literal 'Clients'), this gap means the regression would not be caught by the test suite.

Group-wide canManage() grants manage rights to callers that only have VIEW permission

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key to race

The previous code held `b.cacheMu.Lock()` for the entire `BuildIndex` function, which incidentally serialized all builds for the same NamespacedResource key (even though it hurt cross-namespace concurrency). This PR removes that lock and only takes `cacheMu` around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write (lines 137-139). However, nothing now prevents two goroutines from concurrently calling `BuildIndex` for the *same* key - this happens in practice via `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` (resource/search.go), which is called on every `Search` RPC and on every watch event, and performs an unlocked `GetIndex` read followed by a `build` call on cache miss. If two concurrent requests for a newly-seen (or not-yet-indexed, e.g. small/skipped-at-startup) namespace both see a nil index, they will both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` against the same on-disk directory concurrently (line 98), which can fail or corrupt the index, and will both finish and overwrite `b.cache[key]`, wasting work and potentially leaving an index object whose underlying bleve.Index was already closed/overwritten. This is a regression introduced by the finer-grained locking change, not just a perf improvement.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: moving cacheMu locking from the entire BuildIndex function to only the final cache assignment permits multiple goroutines to concurrently build the expensive index for the same key.

Shared `err` and counter variables mutated unsynchronized across the errgroup goroutines in searchSupport.init

This is a data race: one goroutine's error result can be clobbered by another before it reads it back to return to the errgroup, meaning `group.Wait()`/`s.initErr` can reflect the wrong build's error (masking a real failure or spuriously failing because of an unrelated goroutine's transient error), and `totalBatchesIndexed` can under-count due to lost updates. Because `NewResourceServer` now calls this `init` synchronously at startup (previously it only ran lazily on the first gRPC call), this race is exercised on every process startup instead of occasionally, increasing the chance that a single namespace's indexing error incorrectly fails (or incorrectly succeeds) server construction for all tenants.

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously before returning the constructed server. `Init` calls `s.search.init(ctx)`, which performs a full index build across every namespace returned by `GetResourceStats` using a background context with no deadline. For installations with many/large namespaces this can take a long time (this is literally called out in the PR description as the reason gRPC calls were timing out). Moving this work into the constructor removes the context-cancellation symptom but replaces it with an unbounded blocking call during process/module startup, which can now cause the whole module server (not just a single RPC) to hang past readiness/liveness probe timeouts or deployment rollout windows, with no partial availability and no circuit breaker. This tradeoff (named explicitly as an open question by the PR author: 'What could this break?') should be called out/resolved before merging, e.g. by bounding the startup init with a timeout or making it async with a readiness gate.

Removing per-RPC Init() guards removes the only safety net if initialization wasn't performed

Every RPC method (`Create`, `Update`, `Delete`, `Read`, `List`, `Watch`, `Search`, `History`, `Origin`, `IsHealthy`, `PutBlob`, `GetBlob`) previously called `s.Init(ctx)` defensively before doing any work, which both lazily initialized the server and acted as a guard against using an uninitialized `server` (e.g. `s.broadcaster` being nil, which would be used at `s.broadcaster.Subscribe(ctx)` in `Watch`). The PR fixes `GetResourceStats` (line 126) to reassign `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` so the derived span context is propagated into the subsequent `b.db.WithTx(ctx, ...)` call, matching the PR's stated goal of 'fixing trace propagation by passing span contexts down'. Negative-offset pagination crashes because Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative slice bounds (raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`), so this path will always raise at runtime rather than 'enable efficient bidirectional pagination' as the comments claim ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false). Any admin/superuser request that hits `organization_auditlogs.py` with `optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor whose offset is negative will 500. There is no test exercising this branch, so the bug would ship undetected.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same negative-offset branch in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result(), where advanced features are enabled and cursor.offset is passed as a negative start_offset to QuerySet slicing. The candidate additionally explains the resulting Django runtime error.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared BasePaginator.get_result silently clamps negative offsets instead of erroring, affecting all cursor paginators

`BasePaginator.get_result` (used by `Paginator`, `DateTimePaginator`, and now `OptimizedCursorPaginator` — i.e. most cursor-paginated endpoints in the codebase) used to do `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` directly. The change introduces `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which silently clamps negative offsets to 0 for non-prev cursors instead of letting the previous (implicit) error surface. This changes pagination semantics for every endpoint built on `BasePaginator`, not just the audit log endpoint this PR is nominally about, and ships with no new/updated tests demonstrating the previous vs. new behavior across those call sites.

New admin-gated 'optimized pagination' code path has no test coverage and is unrelated to stated PR scope

A new branch is added that switches to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (with `enable_advanced_features=True`, which enables the broken negative-offset code path) based on a client-supplied query parameter `optimized_pagination=true` combined with `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. This is a brand-new, security-sensitive conditional pagination feature introduced in a PR whose description and other changes are about the spans buffer. No tests were added for this branch, for the permission gating, or for `OptimizedCursorPaginator` itself, so none of this new logic (including the crash described separately) is verified before merge.

Redirect-chain loop bound silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing the explanatory warning comment

The loop that follows redirect pointers (`for i = 0, 1000 do ... end`) was previously bounded at 10000 with a comment explaining that 'segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' The bound was cut to 1000 and the comment was deleted entirely. This makes it 10x more likely that deep redirect/segment trees fail to be joined correctly, and removes the only documentation warning future maintainers about this trade-off, with no corresponding test for deep trees near/above the new limit.

max_segment_spans constructor parameter is now dead code; segment size cap is a hardcoded magic number in Lua, decoupled from configuration

`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans: int = 1001`, but the Python-side enforcement of this limit in `_load_segment_data` was removed entirely in this PR. The new eviction cap is hardcoded as the literal `1000` inside `add-buffer.lua` (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', ...)`), completely independent of `self.max_segment_spans`. Callers who construct `SpansBuffer` with a custom `max_segment_spans` value will silently get no effect from that setting, which is a misleading public API and an operational trap for anyone trying to tune this value.

Unconditional dict indexing on end_timestamp_precise can crash the consumer on payloads missing the field

`process_batch` now does `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` via direct key access with no fallback, where `val` is the raw span payload deserialized from Kafka. If any ingested message lacks this field (e.g. during a rollout where Relay has not yet started populating it everywhere, replay of older backlog messages, or a malformed/older-schema payload), this raises `KeyError` and will crash/raise inside the batch-processing task, taking down the whole consumer batch rather than degrading gracefully. Given this is a critical ingestion pipeline, a schema-evolution-safe default (e.g. `.get('end_timestamp_precise', ...)`) or explicit validation should be used instead of hard failure.

No test coverage for the new eviction behavior, including the risk of evicting the root span's payload

The new eviction logic (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`) removes the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans once a segment exceeds 1000 members. Since the root/segment span can legitimately have an earlier end timestamp than some of its children, it can be evicted by this logic while the separate `has_root_span` flag key still persists, causing `flush_segments` to report a segment as having a root span even though the root span's actual payload was dropped. No test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` exercises a segment exceeding 1000 spans or validates eviction/root-span-retention behavior, so this edge case is unverified.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility check uses the outer closure `dataset` instead of the function's own `scoped_dataset` parameter

Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, ...)`, the call `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` passes `dataset` — the module-level variable computed once in `get()` — instead of the function parameter `scoped_dataset`, which represents the actual dataset being queried for this specific call. In the dashboard-widget-split code path, `_get_event_stats` is invoked multiple times with different `scoped_dataset` values (e.g. `discover` for `errors_only_query`/`transactions_only_query`, or the original `scoped_dataset` for the main query) while the outer `dataset` stays fixed. As a result, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` evaluates against the wrong dataset module for these sub-calls, causing upsampling to be incorrectly enabled or disabled depending on which dataset was resolved at the top of `get()`, producing inconsistent/incorrect counts for dashboard widgets using the discover-split logic.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check receives the outer dataset rather than scoped_dataset, causing incorrect eligibility when dashboard split queries use discover while the original dataset is metrics.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule added, pointing back at the PR's own base commit

This PR adds a new file `sentry-repo` with mode/content indicating a git submodule pinned to commit `a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`, which is exactly the base commit of this same PR. This looks like an accidental artifact (e.g. from a bad `git submodule add` or tooling mistake) rather than an intentional change, has no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry shown, and is unrelated to the stated feature. Merging it risks broken clones/checkouts, confusing repo tooling, and bloats the diff with no functional purpose. It should be removed before merge.

`_is_error_focused_query` inspects the raw request query string, not the effective query used for the specific sub-call

`_is_error_focused_query` (used by `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` for the discover dataset) always reads `request.GET.get("query", "")`, i.e. the original top-level request query. However, `_get_event_stats` is called with different, dynamically-constructed `query` strings in the dashboard-widget split flow (e.g. `errors_only_query = f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"`, `transactions_only_query`). The eligibility check never looks at these per-call query strings, so it can make the wrong upsampling decision (e.g. deciding not to upsample an errors-only sub-query because the raw request query didn't literally contain `event.type:error`, or vice versa).

New `upsampled_count()` SnQL function is not marked `private`, bypassing the allowlist gating entirely

The newly added `upsampled_count` `SnQLFunction` omits `private=True`, unlike the function immediately preceding it in the same list which does set `private=True`. Because it is registered in `function_converter`'s public function map without the private flag, any caller can directly request `upsampled_count()` via the public events/events-stats API (e.g. as `yAxis=upsampled_count()` or in `field`), for any project — not just those in `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`. This completely bypasses the allowlist/eligibility checks implemented in `error_upsampling.py`, which were supposed to be the only gate controlling access to `sum(sample_weight)`-based counts.

Cache key derived from Python's built-in `hash()` risks collisions across unrelated project sets

`cache_key = f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"` uses the built-in `hash()` to fold the sorted project id tuple into the cache key. Distinct sets of project ids can map to the same hash value (hash collisions), which would cause the eligibility decision computed for one set of projects to be served from cache for a different, unrelated set of projects sharing the same organization id, within the 60s TTL. A deterministic, collision-resistant encoding (e.g. a delimited string of sorted ids) should be used instead of relying on `hash()`, which is also not part of any stable contract for this purpose.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is unused dead code — no mechanism actually invalidates the 60s eligibility cache

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined to clear the cached allowlist-eligibility decision "when the allowlist configuration changes," but nothing in this diff calls it (no options-change hook, signal, or admin action wiring it up). Combined with the 60-second cache TTL in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, this means allowlist changes can silently take up to 60 seconds to propagate with no active invalidation path, and the presence of this function creates a false impression that cache consistency is actively managed.

Bare `except Exception: pass` silently swallows all errors when deriving `sample_rate` from event contexts

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps both the dict traversal (`normalized_data.get("contexts", {}).get("error_sampling", {}).get("client_sample_rate")`) and the `float()` conversion in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks. If `contexts` is explicitly `None` (a valid value some code paths may set), `.get(...)` on `None` raises `AttributeError`, which is silently discarded. This means malformed or unexpected test fixture data will silently fail to populate `sample_rate` with no error or warning, making it hard to diagnose test failures or regressions that rely on this helper (used directly by `store_event`, a widely used test utility).

No tests exercise the caching behavior of `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`

The PR title advertises "performance optimizations" via caching, implemented in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (cache hit/miss paths, 60s TTL) and `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. None of these are covered: the unit tests only exercise `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`, `_is_error_focused_query`, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` directly, bypassing the caching wrapper entirely. There is no test verifying that a cached `True`/`False` eligibility value is actually reused on a subsequent call, that it expires correctly, or that `invalidate_upsampling_cache` has any effect.

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the exact literal `count()`, missing aliased or spaced variants

The transform does `if column_lower == "count()":` after lowercasing and stripping, so it only matches an exact `count()` token. Common query shapes like `count() as my_count`, `count(id)`, or any alias form will not be transformed, silently falling back to the regular (non-upsampled) count for those columns while other `count()` columns in the same request get upsampled. This produces inconsistent upsampling behavior across a single request/query without any error or indication to the caller.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New denial-cache test doesn't actually verify the denial-cache short-circuit

In TestService_CacheCheck's 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' subtest, the comment claims 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked', but the permCache entry is set to `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` (an explicit false) rather than `true`. Since reading a missing key or an explicit false both yield `false` from a Go map, and `s.store`/`s.permissionStore`/`s.folderStore` are left as the default empty fakeStore (which returns no permissions and no folders without error), the test would still produce `Allowed: false` via the normal fallback path even if the permDenialCache short-circuit were broken or removed entirely. The test therefore provides no real coverage of the new denial-cache behavior it is supposed to validate.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same inconsistency: the test comment claims cached permissions allow access, but dashboards:uid:dash1 is set to false, so permission checking still denies access. The candidate additionally explains how this undermines the denial-cache test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
userPermDenialCacheKey is vulnerable to key collisions because its fields are joined with '_' without escaping

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates action, name and parent with a plain '_' delimiter: `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Grafana dashboard/folder UIDs are allowed to contain underscores (UID validation permits [a-zA-Z0-9_-]+), so two different (action, name, parent) triples can produce the identical cache key string (e.g. action='A', name='B_C', parent='D' vs action='A_B', name='C', parent='D' both yield '..._A_B_C_D'). Because every denial-cache entry stores the same value (`true`), a collision causes a denial cached for one resource/action to be incorrectly served as a cached denial for a completely unrelated resource/action belonging to the same user, wrongly blocking access that was never actually evaluated, for up to the cache TTL.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-delimited concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey as causing key collisions and incorrect cached permission denials. The candidate describes the same underlying bug and impact.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache can reintroduce the exact staleness bug this PR is meant to fix

The new permission-denial cache (checked at lines 116-121 and populated at line 154) is consulted before the regular permission cache or any DB fallback, and has the same 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) as the rest of the caches. Once a Check() call for a specific (namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder) combination is denied, every subsequent Check() for that exact resource short-circuits to `Allowed: false` for up to 30 seconds, with no invalidation hook tied to permission grants/role/team changes. If a user is denied access to a resource and is then granted access (e.g. shared a dashboard, added to a team, or the permission write for a just-created resource lands slightly after the first check), the user will continue to be denied for up to 30 seconds even though a fresh DB query would now return 'allowed'. This reproduces, for the negative-cache case, the same 'cannot access what I should now have access to' symptom that this PR is otherwise trying to fix by falling back to the DB on cache misses.

Denial-cache hits and permission-cache hits are reported under the same metric labels

In Check(), both a denial-cache hit (line 118) and a positive permission-cache hit (around line 132) increment `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action)`. These are two distinct caches (permDenialCache vs permCache) with different semantics and TT悠L behavior, but the metric conflates them into a single 'cache hit' counter per action. This makes it impossible to measure the effectiveness/behavior of each cache independently from metrics, reducing the observability value that this feature is supposed to add.

List() does not get the same freshness fallback as Check(), so newly created/newly granted resources may still be missing from list results

Check() was changed so that when the cached permission map doesn't grant the specific requested resource, it falls back to a fresh DB query (fixing the 'can't access what I just created' bug for single-resource checks). List(), however, only distinguishes cache-hit vs cache-miss as a whole (lines 180-192): if `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns any cached map at all, that stale map is used as-is to build the list, with no mechanism to detect that it is missing a newly created/newly granted item. As a result, a user who creates a dashboard/folder may be able to directly Check() access to it immediately (via the DB fallback), but the item can still be absent from List() results (e.g. folder/dashboard browse views) for up to shortCacheTTL (30s), partially undermining the stated goal of letting creators see resources they just created.

Removing the client-side cache entirely for in-proc mode increases per-check overhead

The in-proc AccessClient is now constructed with `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})` instead of a real local cache, meaning every single Check/List call from any in-proc caller must always traverse request validation, the in-proc gRPC channel/interceptor, and the server-side cache lookups, instead of being able to short-circuit via a cheap client-side memory lookup as before. For call patterns that issue many repeated/duplicate permission checks in quick succession (e.g. rendering a page that checks access on many individual items), this removes a previously-available fast path and could noticeably increase CPU/allocation overhead, even though the server-side caches still avoid the DB round-trip.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsafe dict access can crash the install pipeline instead of failing gracefully

The new user-mismatch check does `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` using direct dict indexing instead of `.get()`. If an existing `Integration` row (reached via the 'OrganizationIntegration does not exist, but Integration does exist' branch, e.g. a re-install of a previously uninstalled/legacy integration, or one created without full sender data) has a `metadata` dict that lacks the `sender` key or the `sender` dict lacks `login`, this raises an unhandled `KeyError`. That turns what should be a controlled 'Invalid installation request.' error page into an uncaught 500, which directly contradicts the goal of this PR (gracefully rejecting mismatched installs). This should use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and compare, falling back to the error response when missing.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unchecked access to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] and resulting KeyError when sender metadata was not set. Its additional discussion of a missing login key and graceful handling does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Unhandled exception from get_user_info() on GitHub API failure

In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the call `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is not wrapped in a try/except, unlike the token-exchange response parsing just above it (which explicitly catches `Exception` when decoding/parsing the token response). If GitHub's `/user` endpoint returns an error (rate limiting, network failure, invalid/expired token edge cases, etc.), `get_user_info` can raise (e.g. `ApiError`), which will propagate out of the pipeline view as an unhandled exception and produce a generic 500 error instead of the intended friendly 'github-integration-failed.html' error page that the rest of this flow is designed to show.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the scenario it is named for

`test_installation_not_found` stubs a 404 response for `/app/installations/{installation_id}` to simulate GitHub reporting that the app installation cannot be found (originally asserting 'The GitHub installation could not be found.'). After this change, the second request uses `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match `pipeline.signature` (the correct value used elsewhere in these tests is `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). Because `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` checks `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` and returns the generic error immediately on mismatch, the request never reaches the code path that calls `get_installation_info`/`build_integration`, so the stubbed 404 response is never exercised. The test now only verifies the unrelated 'state mismatch' error path while the mocked 404 scenario (and its original purpose) goes untested, and the test's name/setup is misleading about what it actually checks.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup references the literal alias "alias" instead of the actual created IDP alias, leaking test data

In the new testCacheIDPForLogin test, cleanup is registered with `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove);` (also repeated at line 425 for the "idp-alias-20" provider). The literal string "alias" is passed instead of the actual alias used when creating the provider (e.g. "idp-alias-" + i). This means the cleanup never removes the 20+ identity providers created by the test; at best the cleanup call fails (no IDP with alias "alias" exists), and the created identity providers remain in the realm after the test finishes. This leftover state can pollute subsequent tests in the same realm (e.g. IDP count assertions, alias uniqueness on re-run, or other cache tests), causing flaky or order-dependent test failures.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same cleanup bug: using the literal alias "alias" instead of the created provider alias "idp-alias-" + i, preventing proper removal of test identity providers.

false_positives.candidate:
remove() now unconditionally hits the underlying JPA store even when the IDP is already cached

In remove(), `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is now executed unconditionally before the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` check. Previously, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` was only called inside the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` branch; when the cache entry was valid, the code used the already-cached `CachedIdentityProvider` (`cached.getIdentityProvider()`) without touching the delegate at all. After this change, every call to remove() performs an extra round-trip to the underlying storage (JPA/DB) even in the common case where the alias is already present in cache, which is pure overhead introduced only to support the new `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` call. The same information could be derived from `cached.getIdentityProvider()` in the else-branch instead of re-fetching from the delegate, avoiding the redundant query.

No test coverage for invalidating warm login caches via create()/remove() of a currently login-eligible IDP

testCacheIDPForLogin only exercises the create()/remove() invalidation paths (registerIDPLoginInvalidation) with IDPs that do NOT qualify for login (e.g. `testRealm().identityProviders().get("idp-alias-1").remove()` removes a disabled, non-login IDP, and the newly created idp-alias-20 is initially hideOnLogin=true). The 20 initial IDP creations happen before any cache is warmed, so they never actually exercise invalidation of a populated cache either. As a result, the scenario where a currently login-eligible IDP is created or removed after the login caches are already populated (which should trigger registerIDPLoginInvalidation to clear all FetchMode caches) is never verified; only the analogous update() path (registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate) is thoroughly tested. A regression in the create()/remove() invalidation logic for this case would not be caught by this test.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions() contains dead/confusing logic that always returns false

The helper computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then has `if enabled { return false }` followed by an unconditional `return false`. Both branches return false, so the function always disables SQL expressions regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle state. While the intended effect (permanently disabling the vulnerable feature) matches the goal of this security PR, the code reads as though the feature flag controls the outcome when it actually has no effect at all. There is no comment explaining this is a deliberate kill-switch for CVE-2024-9264. A future maintainer could easily 'simplify' this apparent dead code (e.g. by returning `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)` directly) and unknowingly re-enable the vulnerable SQL expression code path, since nothing in the code documents why it must always be false.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that enableSqlExpressions always returns false because both branches return false, unconditionally disabling SQL expressions regardless of the feature flag. The candidate's additional maintenance concerns do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Misleading error message for a feature that is deliberately disabled, not unimplemented

When a SQL expression query is submitted, `ReadQuery` now returns the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". This is inaccurate: the feature was previously implemented and working, and is being force-disabled here as an emergency security mitigation (CVE-2024-9264), not because it was never built. Users/admins who had the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle enabled before upgrading will see a confusing message that doesn't reflect the real reason the feature stopped working, making it harder to diagnose the regression after upgrade.

No tests added or updated to verify the SQL-expressions disablement, likely breaking existing coverage

This PR replaces the DuckDB-backed `DB` implementation with a stub whose `TablesList`, `RunCommands`, and `QueryFramesInto` methods unconditionally return `errors.New("not implemented")`, and pairs it with a reader.go change that unconditionally rejects QueryTypeSQL. No test files are included in the diff, yet pkg/expr/sql/parser.go (table extraction via DuckDB AST parsing) and pkg/expr/sql_command.go (SQL command execution) are exactly the kind of logic that would normally have unit tests asserting successful parsing/execution against a real DuckDB instance. Those pre-existing tests, if they exist, would now fail since every call into the stub returns an error instead of real results, and this PR does not update or remove them. Additionally, for a PR whose explicit purpose is to close an RCE/LFI vulnerability, there is no new regression test asserting that `ReadQuery` rejects SQL expression queries regardless of the `FlagSqlExpressions` toggle state, or that the stub DB always errors. Without such tests, there is no CI safety net to catch an accidental future re-enablement of the vulnerable path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check after acquiring write lock causes redundant work

After acquiring the write lock (line 48-49), the code does not re-check whether entryPointAssetsCache is already populated and the environment is non-Dev before redoing the (potentially expensive) file/CDN read. Multiple goroutines that pass the initial RLock check with ret == nil (e.g. at startup, before the cache has been populated) will each serialize on the write lock and redundantly re-read the manifest file or re-fetch from the CDN, overwriting the cache with the same result each time. This defeats much of the purpose of caching for concurrent initial requests and can add unnecessary I/O latency under load. The fix should re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` right after acquiring the write lock and return early if so.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock in GetWebAssets, allowing concurrent callers to redundantly populate a cache that another goroutine has already populated.

false_positives.candidate:
No test added to verify the data race fix

This PR's stated purpose is fixing a data race in GetWebAssets, but no test (e.g. a concurrent-call test runnable with `go test -race`) was added to verify that the race is actually fixed or to guard against regressions. Without such a test, a future refactor could silently reintroduce the race on the shared entryPointAssetsCache global.

There is a unique index on `embed_url` (see the `create_topic_embeds` migration), so two concurrent calls for the same not-yet-imported URL will race: both see `embed.blank?` as true, both create a Topic/Post, and the second `create!` raises an unhandled DB uniqueness error which rolls back that transaction. Previously, importing a Disqus thread created the topic with `category: category_id` (derived from the `-c/--category` option) and `created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at])`, preserving the original thread date and allowing categorization. `absolutize_urls` treats any `href`/`src` starting with `/` as site-relative and rewrites it to `"#{prefix}/#{href.sub(/^\/+/, '')}"`. For a protocol-relative URL like `//cdn.example.com/image.png`, `start_with?('/')` is true, and `sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips both leading slashes, producing `cdn.example.com/image.png`, which then gets rewritten to `http://<originalhost>/cdn.example.com/image.png` — a broken URL pointing at the wrong host/path instead of the intended external resource. Stale-reminder cleanup runs before cancellation and doesn't exclude cancelled reminders

The first step in this cron handler deletes every EMAIL WorkflowReminder whose scheduledDate is already in the past, without excluding rows that have `cancelled: true` but have not yet been processed by the subsequent SendGrid-cancel step (e.g. because a prior cron run failed to reach them, see the for-loop issue below). Since this deletion runs before the `remindersToCancel` query/cancel loop, any cancelled reminder whose scheduledDate has already slipped into the past gets silently purged from the DB without ever calling SendGrid's cancel endpoint. If SendGrid has not already sent the email by that point, it will still be sent, reproducing exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix.

Single try/catch around the whole cancellation loop aborts remaining cancellations and drops already-queued deletes

The for-loop that cancels scheduled SendGrid sends is wrapped in one try/catch for the entire loop instead of per-iteration. If `client.request` throws for one reminder (e.g. an invalid/expired batch id or a transient SendGrid error), the exception propagates out of the loop, so all remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` for that cron run are never attempted. Additionally, Prisma delete calls are lazy (`PrismaPromise`); the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` calls queued into `workflowRemindersToDelete` for reminders processed before the failing one are never executed because `await Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` is skipped when the exception is thrown. The net effect is that successfully-cancelled reminders can remain in the DB forever as `cancelled: true` (getting re-processed, and re-sent to SendGrid's cancel endpoint, on every subsequent run) and reminders after the failing one in the batch are not cancelled at all during that run, increasing the risk that they later fall into the stale-delete bug above and get purged without ever being cancelled.

remindersToCancel query is missing a method filter

The `remindersToCancel` query only filters by `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate`, without restricting `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. This file is specifically the email-reminder cron job and calls SendGrid's `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` cancel endpoint with `reminder.referenceId`, which for SMS reminders would be a Twilio SID rather than a SendGrid batch id. Currently no code path sets `cancelled: true` for SMS reminders, so this is latent rather than actively triggered, but the missing filter makes the handler fragile to future changes in SMS cancellation logic and is inconsistent with the deleteMany query above it which does filter by method.

File header comment not updated to reflect new cancellation responsibility

The top-of-file comment still reads "Schedule any workflow reminder that falls within 72 hours for email", but this handler now also performs cleanup of stale reminders and cancellation of scheduled SendGrid sends for cancelled/rescheduled bookings (the core fix of this PR). The comment should be updated so maintainers understand the full, and now more safety-critical, responsibilities of this cron endpoint.

No automated tests added for the new cancellation/cron logic

This PR introduces a new `cancelled` field, a deferred-cancellation design split across booking handlers and a cron job, and changes to multiple delete/cancel reminder functions, specifically to fix a subtle production bug (reminders still sent after cancellation/reschedule). No unit or integration tests were added to cover the new cancellation flow (e.g. verifying that a cancelled reminder is actually cancelled via SendGrid before its DB row is purged, or that the cron job doesn't delete unprocessed cancelled reminders). Given the bug class being fixed is timing/ordering-sensitive, the lack of tests makes similar regressions (such as the ordering issue noted above) likely to go undetected.

Unused Prisma import after refactor

`Prisma` is imported from `@prisma/client` (previously used for `PrismaPromise<Prisma.BatchPayload>` typings that were removed in this refactor), but after the change there is no remaining usage of `Prisma.` in this file. Depending on the project's ESLint/TypeScript strictness (`no-unused-vars`), this can fail CI/build linting.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.

Team admin/owner permission check uses AND instead of OR

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. Since `isTeamOwner` is a strict subset of `isTeamAdmin` (an OWNER role satisfies both, but an ADMIN-only role satisfies only `isTeamAdmin`), this expression is effectively equivalent to just `isTeamOwner`. As a result, a team ADMIN who is not also the OWNER, and who is neither the booking organizer nor an attendee, will be incorrectly denied with FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests to a team member's booking, even though team admins should normally have this privilege (as elsewhere in the codebase, e.g. reassign). This should be `||`.

If a user resubmits an email that is already an existing attendee (so it gets filtered out of `uniqueGuests` and not re-added to the DB), that existing attendee's email is still present in `guests`, causing them to incorrectly receive the full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (meant for brand-new attendees) instead of `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`, which is confusing and semantically wrong.

false_positives.candidate:
EventManager built with requesting user's credentials instead of the booking organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` fetches credentials for the user making the request, and `EventManager` is instantiated with `{ ...user, credentials }` where `user` is `ctx.user`. Because the permission check above allows an attendee (not just the organizer) to add guests, when an attendee triggers this flow the calendar sync in `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` will run with the attendee's own (likely absent or unrelated) calendar credentials rather than the organizer's. The booking already fetched `user: { include: { destinationCalendar: true, credentials: true } }` (the organizer), but those credentials are never used. This can silently fail to update the organizer's actual calendar event with the new guests.

Duplicate-guest detection is case-sensitive

`uniqueGuests` is derived by checking `guest === attendee.email` without normalizing case. Combined with the client-side uniqueness check in AddGuestsDialog.tsx (which also does a case-sensitive `Set` comparison), a guest can be added twice with differing email casing (e.g. `John@Example.com` vs `john@example.com`), creating duplicate Attendee rows that represent the same real email address and causing duplicate notifications/calendar invites for what is effectively the same guest.

Email-send failure is swallowed with a bare console.log, losing error details

The `catch (err)` block around `sendAddGuestsEmails` only logs the static string `"Error sending AddGuestsEmails"` via `console.log`, discarding the actual `err` object and bypassing the project's structured logger (`@calcom/lib/logger`) used elsewhere in this same file's imports. This makes it impossible to diagnose production email failures for this flow, and `console.log` (rather than `console.error`/the logger) is inconsistent with how errors are handled elsewhere in the codebase.

No check on booking status before adding guests

The handler fetches the booking and immediately proceeds to add attendees, sync the calendar and send notification emails without verifying `booking.status`. Guests can therefore be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings, resulting in calendar invites and "guests added" notification emails being sent for an event that is not actually happening, confusing invitees and polluting calendars with stale events.

Fallback toast message in onError is dead code

`showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error")` uses `message` which is built from a template literal (`` `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}` ``) and is therefore always a non-empty, truthy string even when `err.data` or `err.message` are undefined (yielding something like "undefined: undefined"). The `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback can never actually trigger, so users may see a raw/unhelpful "undefined: ..." message instead of the intended friendly error text for unexpected error shapes.

isInvalidEmail state is never reset after a successful submission or new attempt

`isInvalidEmail` is only reset to `false` in the Cancel button handler. If a user triggers the "emails must be unique and valid" error once, then fixes the input and successfully submits (via `handleAdd`'s success branch or the mutation's `onSuccess`), `isInvalidEmail` remains `true`. Since the dialog closes on success but the flag is never cleared, reopening the dialog afterward will immediately show the stale invalid-email warning banner even though no new validation error has occurred.

Hardcoded, non-localized tooltip text

The remove-email tooltip uses a hardcoded English string `<Tooltip content="Remove email">` instead of going through the `t()` translation function that is already imported and used elsewhere in this same component (e.g. for "add_another" and the field label). This breaks localization for non-English users of this new shared UI component.

No automated tests for the new add-guests feature

This PR introduces a new tRPC mutation with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer/attendee/team-admin checks), guest deduplication/blacklist filtering, calendar sync, and dual email notifications, plus new UI components (`AddGuestsDialog`, `MultiEmail`). No unit, integration, or component tests are included for any of `addGuests.handler.ts`, `addGuests.schema.ts`, `AddGuestsDialog.tsx`, or `MultiEmail.tsx`, despite the permission-check bug and case-sensitivity issues that tests would likely have caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code validation has a read-then-write race condition allowing double use

In the credentials authorize() handler, a backup code is validated by decrypting `user.backupCodes`, finding the matching index (`backupCodes.indexOf(...)`), and only afterwards persisting the invalidated code back to the DB (`backupCodes[index] = null` followed by `prisma.user.update`). There is no transaction, row lock, or atomic conditional update between the read and the write. Two concurrent login attempts (or an attacker replaying a captured request) using the same backup code can both read the un-invalidated code, both pass validation, and both succeed in logging in before either write completes — violating the single-use guarantee that backup codes are supposed to provide. This should use an atomic update (e.g. a conditional update keyed on the still-encrypted blob, or a per-code DB row with a unique/used flag) instead of decrypt → compute in memory → re-encrypt → write.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same read-then-write race: concurrent login requests can validate the same backup code before its invalidation is persisted, allowing reuse and violating one-time-use semantics.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup codes are stored with reversible encryption instead of a one-way hash

Backup codes only ever need an equality check to be verified (unlike the TOTP secret, which must be decrypted repeatedly to compute codes). Storing them with `symmetricEncrypt` means that anyone who obtains both the database and `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` can recover all ten plaintext backup codes for every user, rather than being limited to verifying a guess as with a proper one-way hash (e.g. bcrypt/sha256 with per-code comparison). Using a one-way hash would reduce the blast radius of a database/key compromise for this specific secret.

Misleading "missing_backup_codes" message tells users to regenerate codes in settings, but no such feature exists

The new string `"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` is shown when a user's `backupCodes` column is null but 2FA is otherwise enabled. However, there is no settings UI or API endpoint added in this PR (or elsewhere) that lets a user regenerate backup codes without fully disabling and re-enabling two-factor authentication (which also resets the TOTP secret). The message gives users incorrect instructions and no actionable path to resolve the error.

No automated test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The PR's own TODO (`// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup`) acknowledges that the actual backup-code authentication paths are untested. `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes `req.body.backupCode` is always a string whenever it is truthy, but request bodies from an API endpoint are not type-checked. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent builds of the same index key to race

The previous code held `b.cacheMu.Lock()` for the entire `BuildIndex` function, which incidentally serialized all builds for the same NamespacedResource key (even though it hurt cross-namespace concurrency). This PR removes that lock and only takes `cacheMu` around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write (lines 137-139). However, nothing now prevents two goroutines from concurrently calling `BuildIndex` for the *same* key - this happens in practice via `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` (resource/search.go), which is called on every `Search` RPC and on every watch event, and performs an unlocked `GetIndex` read followed by a `build` call on cache miss. If two concurrent requests for a newly-seen (or not-yet-indexed, e.g. small/skipped-at-startup) namespace both see a nil index, they will both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` against the same on-disk directory concurrently (line 98), which can fail or corrupt the index, and will both finish and overwrite `b.cache[key]`, wasting work and potentially leaving an index object whose underlying bleve.Index was already closed/overwritten. This is a regression introduced by the finer-grained locking change, not just a perf improvement.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: moving cacheMu from guarding all of BuildIndex to only the final cache write lets multiple goroutines concurrently build the same key's index. The candidate adds call-path and corruption details but points to the identical bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared `err` and counter variables mutated unsynchronized across the errgroup goroutines in searchSupport.init

In `searchSupport.init`, `err` (declared from `stats, err := s.storage.GetResourceStats(...)`) and `totalBatchesIndexed` are captured by every goroutine launched in `group.Go(...)` (lines 186-193) and written concurrently without any synchronization (`totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`), then `err` is read back and returned from each goroutine, and `totalBatchesIndexed` is read after `group.Wait()` for a trace attribute. This is a data race: one goroutine's error result can be clobbered by another before it reads it back to return to the errgroup, meaning `group.Wait()`/`s.initErr` can reflect the wrong build's error (masking a real failure or spuriously failing because of an unrelated goroutine's transient error), and `totalBatchesIndexed` can under-count due to lost updates. Because `NewResourceServer` now calls this `init` synchronously at startup (previously it only ran lazily on the first gRPC call), this race is exercised on every process startup instead of occasionally, increasing the chance that a single namespace's indexing error incorrectly fails (or incorrectly succeeds) server construction for all tenants.

Resource server construction now blocks indefinitely on full search index build with no timeout

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously before returning the constructed server. `Init` calls `s.search.init(ctx)`, which performs a full index build across every namespace returned by `GetResourceStats` using a background context with no deadline. For installations with many/large namespaces this can take a long time (this is literally called out in the PR description as the reason gRPC calls were timing out). Moving this work into the constructor removes the context-cancellation symptom but replaces it with an unbounded blocking call during process/module startup, which can now cause the whole module server (not just a single RPC) to hang past readiness/liveness probe timeouts or deployment rollout windows, with no partial availability and no circuit breaker. This tradeoff (named explicitly as an open question by the PR author: 'What could this break?') should be called out/resolved before merging, e.g. by bounding the startup init with a timeout or making it async with a readiness gate.

Removing per-RPC Init() guards removes the only safety net if initialization wasn't performed

Every RPC method (`Create`, `Update`, `Delete`, `Read`, `List`, `Watch`, `Search`, `History`, `Origin`, `IsHealthy`, `PutBlob`, `GetBlob`) previously called `s.Init(ctx)` defensively before doing any work, which both lazily initialized the server and acted as a guard against using an uninitialized `server` (e.g. `s.broadcaster` being nil, which would be used at `s.broadcaster.Subscribe(ctx)` in `Watch`). These guards are all removed on the assumption that `NewResourceServer` always performs `Init` before returning the server. Any code path that constructs a `server` value without going through `NewResourceServer` (e.g. test helpers within the `resource` package) will now hit a nil-pointer dereference on `s.broadcaster` (or other uninitialized fields) in `Watch`, rather than the previous lazy fallback. The PR description itself raises this exact risk ('Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?') and it isn't verified or addressed in the diff.

The PR fixes `GetResourceStats` (line 126) to reassign `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` so the derived span context is propagated into the subsequent `b.db.WithTx(ctx, ...)` call, matching the PR's stated goal of 'fixing trace propagation by passing span contexts down'. However, the same pattern (`_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)` discarding the new ctx) remains unfixed in other methods in this same file, e.g. `WriteEvent` (line 158), `ReadResource` (line 353), and `ListIterator` (line 388). In each of these, child operations (`dbutil.Exec`, `dbutil.QueryRow`, `dbutil.QueryRows`, nested `WithTx` calls) continue to use the original, non-span context, so trace propagation remains broken for most of the SQL backend despite the PR claiming to address it. This is misleading for anyone reviewing the trace-fix claim and leaves most of the intended fix undone.

The test now unconditionally skips when `GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres` with the comment 'skipping - test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.' This removes postgres coverage for `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` from CI without a linked tracking issue or explanation of what is failing, making it easy for this gap to be forgotten and for a real postgres-specific regression to go undetected going forward.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling assertion is racy and contradicts the test's stated intent

The test's docstring states it verifies "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages," implying the successfully-processed message's offset should still get committed. However the final assertion is `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which actually asserts that NO commit happened. Since `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` completes (and thus makes committable) an offset in its `finally` block regardless of whether `result_processor` raised, both offsets (100 and 101) should become contiguous and committable once both items are processed, and the asynchronous commit loop (`_commit_loop`, firing every 1 second) will eventually commit offset 102. The test's wait loop (max ~0.2-2.2s) races against that 1-second commit cycle: on a fast run the assertion passes merely because the periodic commit hasn't fired yet, not because the intended behavior holds, and on a slower CI run (where the loop takes closer to its 2s budget) the commit may already have happened, making the test flaky/liable to fail intermittently. The assertion does not reliably validate the described behavior either way.
