The candidate elaborates on the resulting race and flakiness, but the underlying issue is the docstring-implementation mismatch.

false_positives.candidate:
close()/terminate() permanently destroy the factory-level shared FixedQueuePool, breaking subsequent Kafka rebalances

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (result_consumer.py lines 131-137) and is meant to live for the lifetime of the factory, the same way `self.multiprocessing_pool` and `self.parallel_executor` do (those are only torn down in `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()`, never by a per-assignment strategy). However, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (line 338) and `.terminate()` (line 342) call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` directly, which permanently calls `Queue.shutdown()` on every internal queue and stops every worker thread in the shared pool. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the currently active strategy and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again on the *same factory instance* on every partition rebalance (not just final consumer shutdown). After the very first rebalance, the shared `queue_pool` is dead: its queues are shut down and its worker threads have exited, but `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` in result_consumer.py (lines 244-259) just reuses `self.queue_pool` without recreating it. Any subsequent `submit()` call on the new strategy will raise `queue.ShutDown` from `work_queue.put()`, which is caught by the generic `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`; that handler then marks the offset as added+completed as if it were processed, even though the message was never passed to `result_processor`. This causes silent data loss for every message after the first rebalance while still advancing committed offsets, defeating the purpose of the feature and corrupting data integrity guarantees.

Use of queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown() requires Python 3.13+

This module relies on `queue.ShutDown` (lines 132, 142) and `queue.Queue.shutdown()` (line 238, called from FixedQueuePool.shutdown at lines 231-243), both of which were only added to the standard library in Python 3.13. If Sentry's runtime is on an earlier Python version (3.11/3.12, which has been the case historically for this codebase), referencing `queue.ShutDown` or calling `.shutdown()` on a `queue.Queue` instance will raise `AttributeError` at runtime, crashing the consumer during normal strategy shutdown/rebalance/termination paths (i.e. the thread-queue-parallel mode would be completely non-functional, not just degraded).

Internal queues have no maxsize, so the advertised "natural backpressure" does not exist

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring (around line 253) claims the strategy provides "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but each per-group queue is constructed as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (line 185), which defaults to an unbounded queue. `put()` therefore never blocks, so there is no backpressure mechanism at all: if one hashed queue backs up (exactly the scenario this PR is meant to mitigate), the consumer will keep reading from Kafka and enqueueing work indefinitely, growing memory without bound instead of slowing down. This contradicts the documented guarantee and creates an OOM risk under the very failure mode the PR targets.

join(timeout) ignores the timeout argument and duplicates close() shutdown logic

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout=None)` (line 345) simply calls `self.close()`, discarding the caller-provided `timeout`. Arroyo's `ProcessingStrategy.join(timeout)` contract is expected to block up to the given timeout waiting for outstanding work to flush before shutdown completes; here the actual draining/joining logic in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (lines 231-243) hardcodes a fixed 5.0 second timeout for both queue draining and worker-thread joins, regardless of what timeout the stream processor configured for graceful shutdown (e.g. `join_timeout` passed through `get_stream_processor`). This can cause premature strategy teardown if more time was actually available, and if `close()` is invoked followed by `join()` (both call the same shutdown path), the second invocation triggers `queue_pool.shutdown()` again on already-shutdown queues, causing extra "Error shutting down queue" exception logs on every normal shutdown.

The `--mode` option's choices were extended to include `thread-queue-parallel` (line 121), but the help string still reads "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." (line 123), which does not mention or explain the new mode's semantics (fixed queue pool with per-group ordering guarantees). Operators using `--help` to choose a processing mode have no way to understand what thread-queue-parallel does or how it differs from parallel/batched-parallel.

The condition for assigning `slug` was changed from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the logic. Combined with the unchanged `requestedSlug` assignment (`...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { requestedSlug: slug } : {})`), when billing is disabled the newly created organization now gets neither `slug` nor `requestedSlug`, so the org has no usable slug at all; when billing is enabled it gets both `slug` and a pending `requestedSlug`, which is contradictory. This change is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (destinationCalendar handling) and looks like an accidental regression from a bad merge/rebase that will break organization creation, particularly for self-hosted instances where billing is disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Hangout link patch call omits the "primary" fallback used for insert

In `createEvent`, the `calendar.events.insert` call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the subsequent `calendar.events.patch` call (to attach the hangout link in the description) uses the raw `calendarId: selectedCalendar` without the same fallback. If no destinationCalendar entry matches the current `credentialId` (so `selectedCalendar` is `undefined`), the insert succeeds against "primary" but the patch call is made with an undefined calendarId, which will fail to update the description with the hangout link.

Organizer email override always uses the first destinationCalendar regardless of which host's credential is creating the event

`mainHostDestinationCalendar` is destructured as the first element of `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar` and used to override the organizer attendee's email (`email: mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId ? mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId : calEventRaw.organizer.email`). When `createAllCalendarEvents` loops over multiple destination calendars/hosts and calls `createEvent` once per host credential, every call still uses the same first-array-entry override instead of the entry matching the `credentialId` actually creating the event (which is correctly looked up a few lines later via `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)`). As a result, for collective events with multiple hosts, every secondary host's calendar event will show the first host's calendar email as the "organizer" attendee instead of their own, undermining the core fix this PR is meant to deliver. The same bug exists in `updateEvent` (lines 198-230) with `mainHostDestinationCalendar`.

Pushing team destination calendars onto evt.destinationCalendar is a no-op when it is null

`destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists (see the ternary ending in `: null,`). Later, `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars);` uses optional chaining, which silently does nothing when `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null`. Consequently, for a COLLECTIVE event where the organizer has no personal destination calendar but other hosts do, all the collected `teamDestinationCalendars` are discarded and only the organizer is considered (incorrectly, with none at all), so secondary hosts never get their calendar invites created — defeating the main goal of this PR in exactly the scenario it is meant to fix.

organization.slug selection dropped from loadUsers query for dynamic bookings

In the refactored `loadUsers` function, the Prisma `select` used for the dynamic/group booking branch (`!eventTypeId`) no longer includes `organization: { select: { slug: true } }`, which was present before this change. If any downstream code in this handler (or in dynamic booking flows generally) relies on `organizerUser.organization?.slug` (e.g., for organization-aware booking links), it will now silently receive `undefined`, changing behavior for dynamic/group bookings tied to an organization without any related test coverage added.

Error logging removed from updateAllCalendarEvents failure path

The previous `console.error(message)` call in the catch block of `updateAllCalendarEvents` was removed when converting the single-reference return to the multi-reference `.map()` version. Errors that occur while updating calendar events (e.g. missing credentials) are now silently swallowed without any log output, making production issues in this path much harder to diagnose.

Inconsistent null vs empty-array representation of "no destination calendar" across code paths

This test now expects `destinationCalendar: []` for the BOOKING_REJECTED webhook payload (produced via confirm.handler.ts, which always falls back to `[]`), while the BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED tests in the same file still expect `destinationCalendar: null` (produced via handleNewBooking.ts, which falls back to `null`). Both represent the same "no calendar connected" state but surface differently depending on which code path produced the CalendarEvent. Since `destinationCalendar` is now a public/typed field consumed by webhooks and third-party integrations, this inconsistency (`null` in some flows, `[]` in others) is a fragile and confusing contract that should be normalized to one representation.

No tests cover multi-host destinationCalendar behavior introduced by this PR

This PR converts `destinationCalendar` from a single object to an array across 22 files and rewrites significant parts of EventManager.ts, CalendarManager.ts, and handleNewBooking.ts's collective-event calendar logic (including the host-list building at this line and the `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...)` call), but the author's checklist explicitly states no tests were added, and the only test file touched (webhook.e2e.ts) merely adjusts one assertion to match the new shape rather than verifying the multi-host calendar invite behavior described as the purpose of the PR. Given the number of latent bugs this refactor introduces (e.g. the no-op push when destinationCalendar is null, and the Google Calendar organizer-override/fallback bugs), the lack of any automated test for the actual collective multi-host calendar scenario is a significant gap for a change of this risk level.

Line 553 changes `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` into `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` to allow the now-async `getCalendar` call on line 556 to be awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Object literal with eager `import()` calls does not provide lazy loading, yet forces async access everywhere

`appStore` is defined as an object literal whose property values are `import("./app")` expressions. Because object literals are evaluated immediately, every one of the ~28 `import()` calls fires as soon as any file does `import appStore from "@calcom/app-store"` (or `@calcom/core/videoClient`, etc.) — exactly as eager as the previous static imports. This gives none of the deferred/on-demand loading benefits typically associated with dynamic import (e.g. `() => import(...)` invoked only when a specific app is actually needed), yet it forces every call site across the codebase (CalendarManager, EventManager, videoClient, handleCancelBooking, handleNewBooking, bookings.tsx, payment handlers, getCalendar) to become `await`-based, adding overhead and the error-handling regressions noted elsewhere in this review, without delivering the stated goal.

No tests added for a cross-cutting async refactor of appStore access

This PR changes the type of every `appStore[key]` access from a directly-usable module object to a `Promise`, forcing `await` in a dozen call sites spanning booking cancellation, rescheduling, calendar, video and payment flows. None of the 12 changed files are tests, and no new/updated tests accompany this refactor. The forEach/async regressions identified in vital/wipemycalother reschedule.ts and bookings.tsx (where error handling silently breaks) would likely have been caught by tests exercising calendar/video deletion failure paths during cancellation/reschedule.

Possible incomplete migration: other appStore consumers outside this diff may still assume synchronous access

The exported shape of `appStore` changed from directly usable namespace objects to `Promise`s that must be awaited before use. Only 12 files are updated in this PR, but `@calcom/app-store` is referenced throughout the monorepo (app installation/configuration flows, OAuth callback routes, admin app pages, event-type app settings, etc.) that are not part of this change set. Any such file that still does `appStore[key].lib...` without `await` will now receive a pending `Promise` instead of the resolved module, which will either fail type-checking (if strongly typed) or silently misbehave at runtime wherever indexing bypasses the type system (e.g. via `any`/loose casts). The PR description and diff don't show that every usage of `appStore` in the repo was audited/updated.

getVideoAdapters now resolves app modules sequentially instead of concurrently

`getVideoAdapters` was converted from a synchronous `reduce` into a `for...of` loop that does `await appStore[appName...]` once per credential (lines 24-33). Since each `appStore[appName]` is a module-level promise, awaiting them sequentially inside the loop adds one microtask tick per credential instead of resolving all of them concurrently with `Promise.all`. For call sites with many credentials (e.g. `getBusyVideoTimes`), this introduces unnecessary sequential latency compared to a `Promise.all(withCredentials.map(...))` approach.
